text:
Years ago, over curries at an embassy dinner, a charismatic Indian ambassador recounted some of his ripsnorting nicknames for fellow diplomats.

The Europeans, in particular the Scandinavians, he dubbed the “Axis of Good” because of smug human rights lectures delivered from high moral pedestals.

Those days might be numbered as European nations seek to borrow from Australia’s offshore immigration detention example and establish so-called return hubs in third countries for people with rejected asylum-seeker claims.

Rwanda and Uganda are in talks to host the centres. (A previous Denmark–Rwanda deal stalled.) Austrian media is reporting that Uganda could initially accommodate up to 10,000 migrants. (Opens in new window) Uzbekistan (Opens in new window) is another country reportedly in the mix.

On Friday, Denmark hosted immigration ministers from Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and Greece for talks, as a dozen demonstrators with megaphones and signs protested outside the Danish parliament.

“We expect to be ready to send the first foreigners to a partner country by the end of next year,” Danish immigration minister Morten Bødskov said, adding he hopes the first deal can be struck around New Year.

The facilities will not be a prison or detention camp, he said.

“It is an agreement with a partner country that gives people that have no legal grounds to be here an opportunity to have a new chance in the partner country,” he said.

The concept has echoes of Australia’s failed resettlement deals with Cambodia (Opens in new window) and Papua New Guinea (Opens in new window).

The five ministers will gather again in Munich later in September for further talks.

Fronting the media after the Copenhagen meeting, they had scant concrete details to share.

They insisted the return hubs “must have a measurable impact on reducing migration and perilous journeys to Europe” and that “Europe’s shared values and human rights must … be reflected in the way these arrangements are designed”.

As a former Canberra Press Gallery reporter who covered immigration at the height of Operation Sovereign Borders, I felt moments of déjà vu as these European ministers parroted lines Australian politicians have used for decades – “breaking the people smuggler’s business models” and “we will decide who comes to our country”.

It remains unclear exactly where duty of care or accountability on human rights violations would lie. The ministers said the International Organisation for Migration and United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees would be involved in monitoring the centres.

One hopes the ministers have done their homework and are taking lessons from Australia’s experience, which the United Nations (Opens in new window), Human Rights Watch (Opens in new window) and Amnesty International (Opens in new window) consider a human rights shitshow.

Denmark’s centre-left Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and her right-wing Italian counterpart Giorgia Meloni have pushed the European Union to take a harder line (Opens in new window) on border security and undocumented migrants and asylum seekers.

The continent is still reeling from the 2015 border security crisis that saw an influx of a million asylum seekers from Syria, Afghanistan and Iraq (Opens in new window).

In June this year, the European Parliament approved changes to migration policy (Opens in new window) to allow member states to set up deportation centres on foreign soil.

Chaotic scenes at Ceuta in August, in which tens of thousands of Moroccans surged into the little-known Spanish enclave in North Africa before being booted out, have also created urgency as far-right parties seek to capitalise on the saga (Opens in new window).

Rights groups are bracing for the worst. Amnesty International said there was a danger the centres “will become places where human rights do not seem to apply” (Opens in new window) and noted the dismal records of Rwanda and Uganda, including the persecution of LGBTQ people in the latter.

Its Netherlands branch described the moves as “a shameless attempt by the EU to shirk its responsibilities regarding migration and shift them onto countries in the South”.

“(European) governments across the political spectrum are now dancing to the same xenophobic and racist tune,” Amnesty NL said.

Other European attempts to send asylum seekers to non-European Union countries have struggled.

Italy has had legal woes (Opens in new window). It had hoped to send 3000 people to Albanian centres but so far only 500 (Opens in new window) have gone at a cost of €670 million (more than A$1 billion) – which is seven times more expensive than an equivalent Italian centre. (Opens in new window)

In 2023, Britain’s High Court ruled that Rwanda was not a safe country for the UK to deport asylum seekers (Opens in new window) arriving on British shores. Former British Labour prime minister Keir Starmer scrapped the deal with Kigali that was set up by conservative leader Boris Johnson’s government. Only four people ended up going to Rwanda and the exercise cost British taxpayers £290 million (A$545 million) (Opens in new window).

The European Union has long considered itself a bastion of human rights and says the bloc’s work “remained grounded in our commitment to protect human rights and democracy”.

“No amount of chaos or conflict will ever change the fact that human dignity, justice and accountability are the only path to peace and prosperity for all,” the EU’s top diplomat said in the foreword of its 2025 human rights annual report (Opens in new window).

But if European countries head down Australia’s asylum-seeker outsourcing path, suicides and self-harm (Opens in new window) are probably inevitable, not to mention the risk of riots and murders (Opens in new window), corruption scandals (Opens in new window) and dodgy contractors (Opens in new window).

Europe’s human rights halo might not be so shiny for much longer.

text:
During the early hours of a recent morning, legal advocates with the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition awakened to buzzing cell phones.

More than 120 men and women had been rounded up by immigration agents inside the Memphis nightclub, El Corralón. Their families and friends needed help.

"Parents didn't come home. Roommates and friends stopped answering the phone. Workers and business owners didn't show up on Monday morning, and cars were left in the parking lot of the nightclub," said Lisa Sherman Luna, the coalition's executive director.

The raid, executed through at least two search warrants obtained by the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation in Shelby County Criminal Court, and reviewed by the Tennessee Lookout, was among the largest immigrant roundups in recent Tennessee history.

The incident occurred amid an escalation in immigrant arrests nationwide that began at the start of summer, following a temporary decline in activity after the January shooting deaths by ICE agents of two Minneapolis residents.

Trump administration officials have touted the immigration crackdowns, in Memphis and elsewhere, as both part of a broader public safety push and a fulfillment of the president's campaign promises to stem illegal immigration.

"Thanks to President Trump's leadership, crime in the city of Memphis has plummeted," a statement from Department of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said recently.

"A big part of that success comes from arresting and deporting illegal aliens in the city," the statement said.

On Thursday, Sherman Luna joined national immigration advocates during a press conference to discuss the Memphis raid and other recent events in Tennessee that, they said, highlight the state's increasingly pivotal role in the Trump administration immigration enforcement and deportation agenda.

The Memphis nightclub raid is among a recent string of events in Tennessee tied to the Trump administration's immigration policies.

In May and June, four Black men were fatally shot in separate incidents by members of the Memphis Safe Task Force, a concentrated crime fighting effort that has brought multiple federal and state agencies, and the Tennessee National Guard, to Memphis. The task force includes Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Homeland Security Investigations, which both enforce immigration law. A Homeland Security Investigations officer fired her weapon during one of the four fatal encounters, according to the TBI. No charges have been brought against officers in any of the fatal shootings.

Late last month, the Lookout first reported the federal government's $63 million contract with the Alaska-based Koniag corporation to establish a 24-7 ICE call center in Tennessee to more closely coordinate with local law enforcement across the country to locate and detain immigrants, including children. (Contract documents initially placed the ICE coordination center in Adams, Tenn., before being updated to reflect Nashville is its planned location).

A spokesperson for Koniag last week did not respond to a request for more information. A spokesperson for ICE declined to discuss details of the planned coordination center.

The federal activities, paired with a slew of state-level legislation introducing immigration status verification into routine interactions with state and local government, "are turning Tennessee into a national hub for the mass deportation machine," Sherman Luna said.

Hadi Sedigh, senior strategist with the National Immigration Law Center, called Tennessee a "testing ground" for the Trump administration as it puts into place similar task force collaborations between federal and local law enforcement elsewhere. Sedigh also highlighted a key priority of the Trump administration to expand so-called 287(g) agreements that delegate immigration arrest powers to local police and sheriffs.

The administration's goal has been codified into law in Tennessee, with legislation enacted this year requiring all sheriffs and police departments to enter the agreements by 2027. Tennessee was among the first states to implement the requirement as part of a package of legislation targeting immigrants that grew out of meetings between Tennessee House Speaker Cameron Sexton, R-Crossville, and White House advisor Stephen Miller.

"The mechanisms that helped make the midnight raid in Memphis possible, namely the 287(g) agreements and the joint federal task force model are, in effect, rapidly increasing in a number of jurisdictions throughout the country," Sedigh said.

text:
PHOENIX — Federal officials have apparently chosen a company with no experience conducting environmental reviews to perform one for a proposed Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facility in Surprise.

In a Friday court filing, the Department of Homeland Security said it has retained a contractor to assist in the review, part of a deal with the state Attorney General’s Office to forestall a lawsuit. That deal prevents ICE from detaining people in the warehouse until DHS can prove it can house up to 1,500 people.

That filing does not list who will be conducting the review. But the city of Surprise, in a web post, said its staffers met with a GardaWorld representative who is seeking information for the assessment.

GardaWord has already signed a $313.4 million contract with DHS to renovate andoperate the facility. The agreement even provides for a possible extension through early 2029, making it worth more than $700 million.

GardaWorld, mostly known for things like providing security guards and operating a fleet of armored cars, referred all questions to Homeland Security.

That agency provided only a prepared statement about its focus on removing “the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens from the United States and is always evaluation the best methods to do so.”

As to the status of the Surprise facility, the statement effectively acknowledges that a federal court agreement with Attorney General Kris Mayes prevents anyone from being housed there until the agreed-to assessment is complete.

“DHS is moving swiftly to utilize EXISTING detention space with our state and county partners,” the statement reads. There was no answer to the question of GardaWorld’s experience — or even confirmation that company is doing the assessment.

Mayes filed suit in April after ICE purchased the facility. That federal ownership stripped city officials of any power to use their own zoning and other laws to restrict its operation.

But the attorney general is instead using the National Environmental Policy Act to require an assessment — if not a full-blown environmental impact statement. And Mayes has made it clear she believes that such an assessment will conclude that the site is inappropriate for such a facility.

That environmental impact is not just about the impact of the facility, like how its operation would affect the city’s sewage. The warehouse itself also sits across the street from a hazardous materials storage warehouse where chemical leaks or explosions are possible.

It is true, Mayes conceded in April, that there already are nearby homes where residents also would be affected by such an occurrence.

“But the major distinction is the sheer number of people who will be housed in this facility and can’t get out,” the attorney general said. “If this thing blows up, they will be locked in that facility with no way of getting out.”

That, she said, will create additional pressures on local fire departments and emergency responders.

And Mayes said the warehouse, if allowed to be used to house ICE detainees, will use so much water that it could leave firefighters without what they need to battle an explosion or blaze at the chemical facility.

The lawsuit initially drew derision from a representative from ICE.

“Let’s be hones about what is happening,” the statement read.

“This isn’t about the environment,” it said. “It’s about trying to stop President Trump from making America safe.”

And the representative dismissed the need for formal environmental studies.

“Prior to purchasing this site, ICE carefully evaluated the use of existing facilities to help minimize environmental impacts,” the statement said.

But facing a possible federal court order delaying — or even halting — the project, Homeland Security said it would provide the assessment. It also agreed not to open the facility until the assessment was completed. And the agency promised to provide regular updates to the court.

That latest update, filed Friday, is where Homeland Security said it had retained a contractor “and has begun working with the contractor.”

“The environmental review remains ongoing,” Julian Kurtz, an attorney with the U.S. Department of Justice, told Judge Susan Brnovich.

text:
A supervisor overseeing background checks warned last year that Immigration and Customs Enforcement was hiring many new officers who had not undergone basic vetting, violating federal rules and putting the agency at risk of misconduct, a newly released whistleblower complaint shows.

The official was a unit chief in ICE's Office of Professional Responsibility, where background checks were backlogged as ICE added thousands of new officers to carry out President Donald Trump's mass deportation campaign.

ICE's human resources division was making final job offers before preliminary vetting steps had been completed, including fingerprints, identity verification and credit checks, the official's complaint warned.

"This unprecedented lowering of standards sacrifices proper risk mitigation for expediency, placing DHS at risk of infiltration and insider compromise," the official wrote in a memo to the Department of Homeland Security's Office of Inspector General dated August 2025.

"This unprecedented lowering of standards sacrifices proper risk mitigation for expediency, placing DHS at risk of infiltration and insider compromise." – Former unit chief, in ICE's Office of Professional Responsibility

The New York Times first reported on the whistleblower complaint Sept. 3. The Associated Press obtained the complaint and a related memo from the now-retired ICE official's lawyer, Kevin Owen. The official's identity was redacted from the complaint. The Times said the official was a 17-year-agency employee and longtime Republican who had voted for Trump in 2020 and 2024.

ICE announced in January that it had hired 12,000 new officers in less than one year, a spree financed by a $75 billion infusion from Congress to increase the agency's arrests and deportations.

The rapid pace of the hiring, fueled by a $50,000 signing bonus, raised concerns about the quality of the new employees. An investigation by The Associated Press found that some of the new hires had serious financial problems in their backgrounds, had been accused of misconduct in prior jobs, and had checkered employment histories.

In July, Tom Homan, the White House border czar, said ICE would investigate apparent shortcomings in the vetting of an officer who shot and killed a 25-year-old motorist in Maine.

The whistleblower complaint said that "systemic breakdowns in vetting" violated several federal rules and standards designed to ensure candidates are suitable for sensitive law enforcement and national security positions.

The complaint said the lack of vetting created "increased vulnerability to insider threats, infiltration and foreign influence," undermined ICE's law enforcement operations and eroded public confidence in the agency.

It asked the inspector general to investigate the personnel vetting failures and for the agency to immediately suspend the improper practices, hold accountable those responsible for the violations and to review all recent hires to identify potential "insider threats."

The Office of Inspector General has previously announced that it is investigating ICE's hiring and training process, as well as security clearances granted to contractors and political appointees.

In a statement, ICE said Sept. 3 the whistleblower was no longer with the agency.

"The ICE Office of Professional Responsibility diligently applies the proper personnel vetting regulations, including guidelines for national security, and evaluates all available information for every applicant based on these factors," the statement said.

As the AP previously reported, ICE acknowledged that some applicants received "tentative selection letters" after their initial applications and interviews. Some were allowed to begin training before their background investigations were completed.

The whistleblower is the second insider to call out ICE's rush to put more officers on the streets as reckless.

A former agency lawyer and instructor at the ICE academy, Ryan Schwank, said the agency cut training on the use of force, firearms safety, and the rights of protesters last year. The Department of Homeland Security has since increased the amount of training for new officers.

___

This story has been updated to correct the spelling of Kevin Owen, not Owens.

text:
A surge in immigration arrests is sweeping up immigrants with no criminal record whatsoever, including many who were already known by the government, as officers push to meet quotas set by the Trump administration.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers broke records for the second Trump administration with back-to-back months of arrests topping 50,000 in July and August.

But the data undercut a long-running claim by the Trump administration that it is targeting the “worst of the worst” by removing those with criminal records.

In fact, more than half of those arrested — 55 percent — had no interaction with law enforcement whatsoever, while another 24 percent have faced charges but were never convicted, according to data obtained by the Deportation Data Project.

These statistics have raised reservations among some Republicans in Congress.

“I’ve been telling the administration that do not conflate the gangster with the gardener, the nanny with the narco,” said Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.), who represents a district where more than half the population is foreign born.

It’s a figure that reflects a growing dynamic in immigration enforcement under the Trump administration — going after those with pending asylum claims or are otherwise seeking to adjust their status who are already known to authorities.

“What this shows is that the Trump administration is expanding its mass deportation operations away from people who are public safety threats or who have had some interaction with the criminal justice system and towards everybody else in an effort to hit the quotas put on them by the White House,” Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, a senior fellow with the American Immigration Council, told The Hill.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has offered mixed messaging on the extent it is still prioritizing criminals for removal.

On social platform X, the department maintains that 70 percent of those arrested by ICE have criminal records — a statement that is demonstrably false based on its own data.

“I mean the 70 percent figure has not been true since May of 2025,” Reichlin-Melnick said.

“DHS has been giving the 70 percent figure for at least a year now. It’s not true. It hasn’t been true. The agency has released extensive data confirming that it’s not true.”

But in media appearances, leaders have also distanced themselves from stressing the importance of arresting criminals, even as media releases from the agency continue to tout deportations of “the worst of the worst.”

“These individuals that we’re going after — I don’t care if you have a criminal background or don’t have a criminal background, you chose to break the law when you came across our border illegally. It’s our position and our job to hunt you down and send you back to where you came from,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said this past week during an appearance on “The Ingraham Angle.”

Border czar Tom Homan also contradicted the DHS’s claims during an appearance on the same show in July.

“Just over half of everybody we’re arresting is a criminal. So about half are noncriminals,” he said.

“But bottom line is, everybody’s on the table. The numbers show it’s about half and half now. … And with the additional resources we got from the reconciliation bill, you wait to see what the numbers are this year.”

There have been several factors behind the uptick in arrests, from a stealthier approach to enforcement under Mullin that departed from the widely publicized raids used previously to more recent tactics like arrests of immigrants at airports.

“This is from all the different tactics coming together really for the first time. The street arrests happening at the same time you have all the check-ins for people, immigration court interactions. All that stuff’s coming together — the airport arrests,” said David Bier, director of immigration studies at the libertarian Cato Institute.

Bier noted that Mullin got to the department as “all these resources [were] coming online at the same time.”

“They’re paying people a huge amount of overtime. They have no worries about money, so you know that’s a big part of it too is they just have people working like crazy to get these through,” he said.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal (Wash.), the top Democrat on the House Judiciary subcommittee on immigration, said the less overt operations carried out by Mullin are in part due to the backlash to the much publicized raids carried out under former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem.

“They are continuing this strategy quietly now because it was unpopular when it was loud. But they’re going to find out in November that it’s unpopular when it’s quiet as well,” she told The Hill.

“They’re just arresting anyone. It’s just all about their ultimate number.”

Reichlin-Melnick noted that many of those being arrested, beyond having no criminal record, are also people who are already in immigration processing.

“We’re seeing this expanded to people at airports, people who overstayed their visa solely because the U.S. government didn’t get around to adjudicating their case in time, and these are people who really have done nothing wrong. They took the path that the Trump administration itself used to say was the right way,” he said.

“More and more of those people are now being swept into the mass deportation machine, despite the fact that they have pending applications with the U.S. government and have been complying with every obligation put on them. So why is the administration going after them? Because in some ways they are the easiest targets. They tell the government who they are or where they live. … And so when the U.S. government needs to ramp up arrest numbers, it can just go after those people rather than having to find people that it doesn’t know about already.”

Bier noted the increase in the number of those arrested without a final order of removal — an order given by an immigration judge after determining someone should be deported — leaving them waiting in detention as they continue to fight their case.

“Pretty soon, it’s going to be a majority of their deportations are not going to be based on a final order of removal, which will be just a real threshold for proving the success of the strategy, which is arrest and detain people without removal orders, and then just hope they give up,” he said.

The surge in arrests has led to some backlash, even in solidly red Florida, where immigrant communities include naturalized citizens as well as those who do not have status.

“Look, I’ve always supported TPS for Venezuelans, for Haitians,” said Rep. Mario Diaz-Balart (R-Fla.), referencing the temporary protected status program that protects people who are otherwise deportable from being sent back to countries that are considered dangerous.

“Securing the border had to happen. It’s worked. It’s good. It’s good for our security. But some of the enforcement, I think, has been a bit of an overreach, to say the least — to say the least. I’ve expressed that.”

“You can enforce the border, but I think you also have to hopefully look at all the circumstances when you have some specific cases,” he added.

Salazar, who has sponsored the Dignity Act as a way to help those without legal status gain a pathway to remain in the country, said the administration has failed to account for the economic contribution made by those without criminal records who have been working in the U.S. for years.

“The people who’ve been here for decades in construction, hospitality, agricultural, healthcare, manufacturing [industries] — those people are needed, and we need it for the economy. It’s just that there is a disconnect. … The White House is not understanding that those people are needed for the economy,” she said.

“And that those are our values as Americans.”

text:
Protesters gathered Saturday to make their presence known after increased activity from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement was witnessed across Indianapolis this past week. They met near the federal agency's west side office.

The weekend protest followed two other demonstrations held at a hotel less than half a mile from the ICE office.

The increased ICE activity seen in Indianapolis coincides with a record-high number of arrests made by ICE in July, nearly 50,000 across the country, according to data gathered by the Deportation Data Project based at U.C. Berkeley and UCLA.

An unidentified spokesperson from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security did not answer questions sent by WFYI asking for the number of arrests made in Indiana this past week, or provide confirmation of increased enforcement operations in Indianapolis. They did reiterate their goal, at the directive of President Donald Trump, to deport criminals and anyone who entered the country illegally.

Saturday's demonstration at the ICE office attracted over 100 protesters who oppose the influx of arrests and detainments witnessed through social media posts.

ICE agents and other law enforcement have been seen making arrests in residential neighborhoods, gas stations and other areas across the city.

Jesus Ramirez has been a community organizer and activist fighting for immigrants' rights in Indiana for years. He said a few concerned individuals organized Saturday's protest, not a single organization.

"It's one of those things where as long as [ICE is] going to continue terrorizing our people, we're going to continue to be in front of your building, being as loud as we possibly can to let you know that we're not moving," Ramirez told WFYI.

Ramirez said he knows some of the individuals recently arrested or detained by ICE. He believes the arrests have been racially motivated and that the agency is no longer focused on getting "the worst of the worst."

"The collateral damage that we're seeing is bigger than if they're going for one person supposedly with a warrant, and there's six other people around that have nothing to do with it," Ramirez said. "They're getting dragged along with no due process."

Ramirez said he's spoken with families who said they're afraid to get groceries or send their kids to school.

An analysis done by the New York Times on ICE arrests found that a majority of immigrants arrested in July had not been charged with or convicted of a crime, but were accused of violating civil immigration laws.

Noise protests

On Thursday evening people arrived at a Hampton Inn, less than half a mile away from Indianapolis' west side ICE office, where organizers believed ICE agents were staying as guests.

"It's a noise rally, basically, to make sure that they feel very unwelcome, that they feel very uncomfortable, and that they don't have a moment of peace while they're here terrorizing Indianapolis residents," organizer Stephen Lane, who is with the Indianapolis Party for Socialism and Liberation, told WFYI at the protest.

WFYI did not confirm whether ICE agents stayed at the hotel or not.

After the sun set, over 50 people were spread across the lawn in front of the hotel lobby. Organizers with megaphones led the demonstration in chants, including "ICE out now!" and "Chinga la migra!" Some had musical instruments — horns, a trombone and a saxophone — and played a beat on makeshift drums and bells.

Lane said he's been checking on immigrant residents he knows in Indianapolis since arrest reports picked up.

"To see that they have to go through this, these raids in our communities, in our neighborhoods — it makes me sick seeing it happen all over the internet. I know that some people are hiding their immigrant neighbors in their house, like this is 1945 Germany," Lane said. "It's ridiculous."

Some honked their cars while parked across the street. Others revved engines in the hotel parking lot. Semi-trucks and cars honked as they passed.

An officer with the Indianapolis Metropolitan Police Department was dispatched to the hotel. Later, more IMPD officers arrived, Lane told WFYI. He said they told protesters the hotel wanted them to leave, and that they would violate a noise ordinance after 11 p.m. Lane said they decided to go home, then Friday morning around 6 a.m., a smaller crew set up across the street.

At the protest at the ICE office Saturday, Angelica Rabell said she felt like she needed to come because of the way she's seen ICE officers treat immigrants, including legal citizens.

"Not only that, they had deported two people that I've known very close to me without any reason, and they also invaded the personal space of my own family members a few days ago," Rabell said.

She said everything she's seen in the past week has made her feel frustrated, and worried for those who don't yet have full legal status. Rabell held a sign that read "no one deserves to die at the hands of ICE."

Contact WFYI Government Reporter Caroline Beck at cbeck@wfyi.org

text:
By Jongwon Lee, American Community Media

SAVANNAH, Ga. — Kim vividly remembers the Sept. 4, 2025 ICE raid on the Hyundai-LG battery plant in Georgia. Working in an office near the facility, she learned from a coworker that the plant was surrounded by helicopters and military-style armored vehicles.

She turned on the television and saw news coverage of workers being handcuffed and shackled. By the end of the day, several of her coworkers had not returned to the Savannah-area joint-company plant, which was still under construction at the time.

When Kim — who asked to be identified only by her last name — drove to the plant after the raid, she found the parking lot filled with hundreds of empty vehicles.

“It was like the aftermath of a war zone,” she recalled.

Working as a human resources manager for an LG contractor which mobilized staff to help detainees, Kim spent hours every morning over the week following the raid outside the Folkston ICE Processing Center seeking visitation with detained colleagues.

“Some days, visitation was denied, or abruptly canceled after an hour or two without explanation or notice,” she said.

Her duties also included retrieving abandoned vehicles, contacting detainees’ families in South Korea and packing personal belongings — tasks she described as painful.

Ultimately, more than 300 South Korean nationals were released and returned to South Korea after eight days in detention.

When construction of the battery plant was completed in early 2026, Kim sold her home in Georgia and moved to Texas to work at another technology facility.

She said she had little optimism left for her future in Georgia, noting that Texas had not taken similar enforcement actions against invited foreign investors.

She noted that the experience left a lasting impact, leading her to refrain from international business travel to Mexico despite holding legal U.S. immigrant status for years.

Aftermath of the ICE raid

One year after the enforcement action, construction on the Hyundai-LG battery plant is finished. The Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America (HMGMA) appears fully operational, following executive announcements targeting increased production in Georgia.

However, a few blocks behind the facility, an Asian grocery store that once sold kimchi and ramen to workers has closed. Local resident Morgan Foreman noted that the store shut down months after the raid.

Local Korean restaurant owner Moon — who asked to be identified by his last name — noted that abandoned and returned items, including boxes of Korean ramen, accumulated at customer service centers in local grocery stores after Korean workers suddenly departed following the raid.

The raid also heavily impacted non-Korean workers.

According to Jenny Miron of local non-profit Migrant Equity Southeast (MESE), at least 175 Latino workers — primarily from Venezuela — were detained.

Following the release and departure of the South Korean workers, only nine Latino workers are known to have been released through legal support from organizations like MESE. The remaining workers were deported, removed, granted voluntary departure or opted for self-deportation.

“Many Latino workers still remain in legal limbo and face pressure to leave the country,” Miron said.

She added that heightened ICE activity and police presence have contributed to financial hardship and legal uncertainty among affected families: “Community organizations have had to step in with direct support, including gift cards, food boxes, transportation and pro bono legal assistance to help families stay afloat.”

A continued atmosphere of fear

A year after the raid, ongoing enforcement activities continue to cause concern among workers in coastal Georgian communities like Savannah.

Miron noted that heavy police presence and ICE activity have created an atmosphere of fear, leaving some community members hesitant to go to work, shop for groceries or drop their children off at school.

Similar concerns have been raised in metro Atlanta.

Eulen Jang, policy advocacy manager at the Asian American Advocacy Fund (AAAF), addressed the DeKalb County Board of Education on Aug. 10, urging officials to protect students from ICE activities within the district.

“This isn’t a political issue; it’s a student safety issue and an immigrant rights issue,” Jang testified.

She added: “There are many instances of ICE agents showing up at homes, worksites, and other locations without presenting a warrant, or using documentation that is legally insufficient. It can be intimidating to staff members if ICE shows up to a school while personnel are unclear about district procedures or how to verify legal authenticity.”

On Aug. 7, three days before Jang’s testimony, ICE announced the arrest of 1,226 individuals across Georgia as part of an enforcement initiative designated “Operation Safe Community — Atlanta.”

According to ICE statements, 720 of those arrested had prior criminal charges or convictions in the United States, while the remaining 506 had no criminal records but were cited for immigration violations.

The recent ICE operations in metro Atlanta have drawn public scrutiny.

On Aug. 11, WSB-TV reported that ICE agents mistakenly handcuffed a U.S. citizen, John Phillips, on a jet bridge at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport.

ICE later confirmed that agents were searching for a British national with the same name and date of birth.

Local law enforcement agencies have noted a lack of direct coordination with federal officers.

During an Aug. 12 “Coffee with a Cop” event with members of the Korean community, representatives from the Duluth Police Department stated that they had not been contacted nor consulted by ICE regarding recent arrests in metro Atlanta.

In both coastal Georgia and metro Atlanta, community members state that systemic issues remain unresolved a year after the ICE raid in Georgia.

Corey Foreman, a Savannah-area businessman and Democratic candidate for the state Senate, characterized the 2025 raid as more of a “media stunt” than a targeted immigration operation, noting that “many workers were on valid visas for technical setup rather than permanent immigration.”

He added that public updates and media coverage ceased shortly after the raid, leaving residents with little information regarding subsequent developments.

Miron expressed concern over the persistent “status quo” one year later, emphasizing the role of community support, social media campaigns and donations in providing essential food, transportation and legal assistance.

“Solidarity gives our immigrant communities hope,” Miron said. “Even as the political landscape changes daily, knowing there are people willing to offer support encourages individuals to speak out and help one another.”

title: Horsey's ICE column hides who's being arrested - Seattle Red
description:
“Like nearly all the people being pulled off the street, locked up and separated from their families by ICE, Sidhe has no criminal record,” Horsey wrote in a clumsy column titled “ICE comes for our neighbors in WA.” Nearly all?
That is the rhetorical beam holding up the entire column, and it’s not true.
Indeed, that reality was recently reported in the Seattle Times itself.
The neighbors Horsey deleted from the story There are plenty of places to get the truth on who is being arrested and detained.
ICE Seattle announced eight arrests in a single week this summer, and the records were public.
text:
David Horsey framed his latest Seattle Times column and cartoon around Robert Sidhe, a University of Washington Medical Center patient care technician now held in Tacoma, and then used that one man to describe every arrest Immigration and Customs Enforcement makes in Washington. The argument only holds up if the convicted sex offenders, fentanyl dealers and repeat drunk drivers sitting in the same facility vanish. Horsey makes them vanish with a single clause.

“Like nearly all the people being pulled off the street, locked up and separated from their families by ICE, Sidhe has no criminal record,” Horsey wrote in a clumsy column titled “ICE comes for our neighbors in WA.” Nearly all? That is the rhetorical beam holding up the entire column, and it’s not true. Indeed, that reality was recently reported in the Seattle Times itself.

A columnist arguing in good faith would tell readers who else is in that building. Horsey names one man and hopes nobody checks because he’s not offering an argument in good faith. He rarely does.

The neighbors Horsey deleted from the story

There are plenty of places to get the truth on who is being arrested and detained. ICE Seattle announced eight arrests in a single week this summer, and the records were public.

Alan Gomez-Everisto, 36, of Mexico, holds a felony conviction for controlled substance homicide involving a minor; police say he gave fentanyl to a 15-year-old boy who died hours later. Patrick Popowski, 41, was required to register as a sex offender after pleading guilty to assault and communicating with a minor for immoral purposes. Angel Colin-Enzana, 55, was arrested by the King County Sheriff’s Office for rape and kidnapping in 2003 and later convicted of assault in Snohomish County. All three went to Tacoma. ICE published the rap sheets while Seattle columnists looked away.

So ask Horsey the question his column exists to avoid. Does he want the man convicted in a teenager’s fentanyl death living next door to him? The registered sex offender? If the answer is no, why write a column insisting those men are imaginary?

The Gestapo line gives away the tired strategy

Horsey did not stop at sympathy, of course. He has to demonize.

“Immigration and Customs Enforcement has done a better job avoiding attention lately, but America’s immigration Gestapo has not backed off from enforcing the Trump administration’s disgraceful war on immigrants,” he wrote.

“Anyone who voted for this president and his immigration policy should be ashamed,” Horsey added.

Nazi secret police. Shame on your neighbors. That is what passes for immigration analysis at the Seattle Times, and it depends entirely on readers never learning who fills the beds at the Tacoma Detention Center.

Here’s the truth

Federal prosecutors keep telling Washington what deportation actually interrupts.

Two illegal immigrants were sentenced this summer for illegally reentering the country, and First Assistant U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd was direct about the pattern behind those cases.

“Both of these defendants were removed from the U.S. and returned illegally multiple times,” Floyd said. “They were encountered by local law enforcement multiple times, and in each case, they were released back into the community to commit additional crimes, including violent assaults.”

Horsey can have the asylum case. Argue it, litigate it, win it, I guess. He does not get to pocket the sympathetic detainee and then tell Washington that the fentanyl dealer, the rapist and the repeat illegal reentrant were never arrested at all. Washington politicians have spent two years selling that same fiction. Horsey just draws it better, though barely.

text:
NEWPORT, Maine (WVII) -- State representatives have confirmed that U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) will be leasing a building in Newport.

The location is 12 Water Street in Newport, the site of the former Newport District Court that had to close last year due to a mold infestation.

Newport legislator Kenneth Fredette explains that not much is known about ICE's plans for the facility. Philipps Representative Mike Soboleski confirmed the plans in a Facebook post after touring the Scarborough processing facility, saying quote, a new ICE facility will soon be under construction at the former Newport district courthouse and will help the deportation process move even faster," end quote.

"I've spoken to people that have indicated that ICE would be using this building as probably some sort of administrative type building," said Rep. Fredette. "In my opinion, to the extent that they're spending money in the local economy and again doing their job in a peaceful manner and a respectful manner, I think that's what's important."

According to Fredette, due to the former courthouse's small size and limited space, it's very unlikely to be a detention or processing facility unless more construction is done.

"It's not a facility where you could hold anybody as a detention facility. It really has some conference rooms and a courtroom, I believe it would be merely administrative in nature," he added.

The building has been vacant since January 2025, with Fredette saying the mold issue is believed to have been resolved.

"Really it's not a public issue, it's a contractual issue between the landlord and the tenant," Fredette stated.

The presence of ICE officers in Maine has been controversial, mostly starting with ICE's "Operation Catch of the Day" immigration enforcement effort in January 2026, taking place across the state.

Fredette remains hopeful that the building's use will not prove contentious in the area: "We live in a period of political rage, and really what we need to be doing is living in an era of political respect...I think people really just need to be following the law ,and if people are following the law I think everyone is going to be just fine."

However, locals seem to be somewhat split on the facility and the topic.

"I'll tell you right now, if you have people that come here, want to work, make an honest living, why do we want to kick those people out? They need to stay...when someone's working hard, doing what we want them to do, doing the jobs we don't want to do, I'm okay for those people staying here," shared Glenburn resident Anthony Campbell.

"If they have a place to take them to until they can get them back to their own country, I think that's great. I think all the ones that came in illegally should go back to where they were and come back through the proper channels," stated Vicki Savage of Plymouth.

Also read: Rep. Pingree speaks out against plans for new ICE facility in Maine

We have reached out to ICE but have yet to hear back at this time.

title: Shapiro hires ex-Trump admin official to help counter president's 'attacks' | 90.5 WESA
authors: Angela Couloumbis | Spotlight PA, www.wesanews.org, angela-couloumbis-spotlight-pa
description:
Josh Shapiro made an unconventional hire: a senior advisor to help him deal with the Trump administration.
In August, Shapiro joined a coalition of state attorneys general suing the federal government over the subpoena.
For his part, Shapiro often talks about how his administration has sued Trump dozens of times to challenge the loss of federal funding.

The Trump administration sold MPP as a way to thwart people with fraudulent claims from easily entering the U.S.
text:
Earlier this spring, with no public notice, Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro made an unconventional hire: a senior advisor to help him deal with the Trump administration.

Jennifer Higgins, a longtime federal immigration official based in Washington, D.C., was brought on to help Shapiro and state agencies under his jurisdiction map out responses to some of the president’s targeted attacks on Democrat-led states — notably, funding cuts and demands for sensitive or proprietary information.

Higgins is being paid by the hour — an unusual arrangement for a gubernatorial staffer, and one that Shapiro’s office could not immediately explain. State payroll records show she is paid $89 per hour, and Shapiro officials said she works full-time, putting her annual salary at roughly $185,000.

The administration defended hiring Higgins, even though Pennsylvania already spends tens of thousands of taxpayer dollars every year for a federal government liaison.

The governor’s office employs a full-time lobbyist in Washington, D.C., who is paid $177,507 annually. And in theory, Pennsylvania’s two senators act as the state’s de facto protectors in the nation’s capital and run interference with the White House when problems arise.

But Shapiro spokesperson Rosie Lapowsky explained in an emailed statement that an additional person was needed because “the Trump administration’s relentless attacks on the rights and freedoms of Pennsylvanians are reaching into every corner of our Commonwealth.”

Higgins, Lapowsky said, brings “deep expertise and invaluable perspective helping protect Pennsylvanians during this critical moment.” (Higgins did not respond to Spotlight PA’s request to speak with her directly.)

Still, Higgins’ expertise is in the immigration sphere, where she has spent nearly the entirety of her career. The governor’s office acknowledged that Higgins is not directly advising Shapiro on immigration issues, but is part of a larger group of policy officials, lawyers, and others who provide the governor with information on that and other issues facing the state.

Asked for an example of Higgins’ work, Lapowsky said she helped coordinate Shapiro’s response to a Trump administration demand that states turn over commercial driver's license records containing personal information. Trump officials have pointed, among other things, to crashes involving noncitizen drivers as one reason for the crackdown and have threatened to withhold federal funding if states do not comply.

In August, Shapiro joined a coalition of state attorneys general suing the federal government over the subpoena.

It’s true that, since reclaiming the White House in 2024, President Donald Trump has used the levers of the federal government to punish blue states.

The administration admitted in a federal court filing this summer that it recommended scrapping billions in grants for clean-energy projects based solely on those states’ “political identity,” and whether Trump won the vote in those places in the 2024 election.

Earlier this year, Trump attempted to freeze billions in childcare and social assistance for five Democratic-led states — he had initiated the move following the federal fraud probe involving Minnesota’s social services network — which he later abandoned.

And Politico reported last month that Trump overruled his own emergency management agency to deny federal relief funds to four Democratic-led states.

For his part, Shapiro often talks about how his administration has sued Trump dozens of times to challenge the loss of federal funding. Those suits involve a range of initiatives, from education to natural disasters. The governor’s office also noted that unlike in other states, where attorneys general are handling litigation against Trump, Shapiro’s lawyers are taking on that work in Pennsylvania. Attorney General Dave Sunday, a Republican, has not entered the commonwealth into any lawsuit against the president or his administration.

Many of those suits predate Higgins’ arrival, and were handled by attorneys already on Shapiro’s staff. But the volume of attacks coming from Washington, Lapowsky said, combined with the range and breadth of policies and issues being targeted, necessitated another person to help coordinate plans to respond.

Immigration leadership

Higgins’ role in the Shapiro administration differs significantly from the work that has defined her career.

She started as an immigration officer in the early 2000s, but quickly moved into leadership roles within the federal office that handles asylum applications and screenings and adjudicates refugee applications, according to an online biography.

Shortly after Trump was elected to a first term in 2016, Higgins became the office’s associate director. Some rights groups have highlighted that part of her bio, since she held a leadership position during the implementation of one of the federal government’s most controversial immigration programs.

Officially called the Migrant Protection Protocols (MPP), but better known as Remain in Mexico, the program went into effect in early 2019. It required asylum seekers along the southern border to return to cities in Mexico, many of which are dangerous, while waiting for their immigration cases to be heard in the courts. Previously, those people were allowed to stay in the United States during that waiting period.

The Trump administration sold MPP as a way to thwart people with fraudulent claims from easily entering the U.S. But human rights and immigration groups, as well as multiple news organizations, extensively documented how migrants sent to Mexican border towns faced extreme danger, including kidnapping, assault, and rape. Tent camps were set up to house some of the asylum seekers, but living conditions were squalid, with no running water or electricity.

Human rights groups also noted that access to legal representation was fraught with obstacles, and resulted in higher numbers of cases being denied, sometimes just because migrants did not receive timely notices of their hearings or could not safely reach ports of entry into the country to be present for such hearings.

The office where Higgins held a senior leadership role at the time — the Refugee, Asylum and International Operations Directorate (RAIO) inside the U.S. Department of Homeland Security — was part of the larger apparatus tasked with the MPP’s rollout. Higgins’ level of involvement in the program’s operations is not clear, as the office’s work is subject to high levels of confidentiality. But the office she helped oversee is responsible for, among other duties, conducting asylum screenings and applications, according to its website. Its employees would have been at the front lines of the program’s implementation.

President Joe Biden ended the Remain in Mexico program after defeating Trump in 2020. Since retaking the White House, Trump officials have attempted to revive it but have been blocked by the courts.

During Biden’s presidency, Higgins continued to rise. She became acting chief of staff to then-U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas, and within a year was appointed acting director of the department’s vast agency that oversees the legal U.S. immigration system.

Shortly after Trump started his second term, she was replaced.

EB: The conditions at the detention facilities vary based on where you are.
text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has released its latest batch of nationwide detention statistics that show Wisconsin arrests by ICE agents hit new highs in June and July.

The number of arrests jumped from at least 119 in May to 220 in June and were concentrated in the southeastern portion of the state. Since January 2025, the start of President Donald Trump’s second term, more than 2,100 people have been detained in Wisconsin.

That is all according to a new data analysis from Paul Kiefer, a fellow at Wisconsin Watch who focuses largely on immigration and data reporting.

The reporting showed that although 70 percent of these arrests happened in Wisconsin jails or prisons, there is an increasing number of arrests occurring in people’s homes, on the streets or at a courthouse.

“There was a flood of social media footage of officers pulling their targets out of cars, pulling up in their driveways in suburban Milwaukee,” Kiefer said on WPR’s “Wisconsin Today.” “That was a departure from the prior year and a half of arrest patterns.”

To hear more about the impact of these arrests, WPR spoke with Erin Barbato, the director of the Immigrant Justice Center at the University of Wisconsin Law School.

The following conversation has been edited for clarity and brevity.

Kate Archer Kent: We see this spike in June arrests in Wisconsin remaining elevated in July. How is this surge in ICE arrests impacting your clients?

Erin Barbato: From what I observed the number didn’t surprise me because we are deep into responding to many of the arrests and also serving the people that are detained here in Wisconsin.

But the fear that people have to live with — that they could be picked up off the street without having done anything wrong, just living their lives, going to work, taking their children to school — has been really difficult for our communities and harmful to families that live here in Wisconsin.

KAK: The data indicates that some people are being arrested at the Department of Homeland Security field office in downtown Milwaukee, where ICE agents arrest people during mandatory check-ins. What are these check-ins?

EB: Some people who are in removal proceedings might be able to live in the community while those proceedings are going forward.

Because of the backlog in immigration court, it may take a few years for people to get in front of an immigration judge. During that time, they may have to check in with ICE just to confirm that they’re still here, they’re not a flight risk, they’re not doing anything nefarious. It used to be pretty routine, you would check in, make sure the officer knows your current address and if anything else has changed, like your job.

But now they’ve turned into a time when people are terrified to attend because there doesn’t seem to be any sort of rhyme or reason why one person may be detained and another is not. So people go in there quite blind in terms of what is going to happen to them. They could be leaving that day, or they could be leaving and returning to their family, or they could be put in detention and permanently separated from their family.

KAK: As for the data indicating more than half of the people detained from Wisconsin have a criminal record, some people would say, “Look, ICE is fulfilling its purpose here.” What do you make of that argument?

EB: If you look at it just on the surface, that argument makes sense. However, once people see what we’re considering as criminal records, many of these people have not done anything dangerous or not done anything that would make someone uncomfortable.

For example, people without status here in Wisconsin can’t obtain driver’s licenses. We do not have a vast public transit system here in Wisconsin, many people have to drive to work, and they can’t drive to work without driving without a license because they can’t get one.

KAK: I want to land on what detention might mean for someone. We saw Lianyong Wei, the Chinese immigrant, die in ICE custody on Aug. 23. It’s marking the 57th person to die in the care of government since the start of President Trump’s second term, and that’s according to ICE’s detainee death notifications. What are conditions like at detention facilities now?

EB: The conditions at the detention facilities vary based on where you are. Some of the detention facilities can hold over 1,000 people. Some have space for much less. But some of the facilities — I recently visited one in Texas that is basically a tent city — they don’t have the infrastructure or protection that is humane or safe for people to live in.

We constantly hear worries from our clients that aren’t getting their medication. We have a client who has diabetes and she’s had a really difficult time getting her medication, which is terrifying and unfair and unlawful, in my opinion.

text:
The family of a man falsely and publicly accused by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) of threatening the president’s life is preparing to sue the federal government for intentionally lying about their father, creating a climate of fear and setting off a wave of harassment.

On May 22, 2025, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested Ramon Morales Reyes, 55, a Mexican immigrant living in Milwaukee. The agency made the arrest after receiving a handwritten note, ostensibly signed by Morales Reyes, threatening to shoot the president.

DHS posted his mugshot online alongside a message from then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem proclaiming, “Thanks to our ICE officers, this illegal alien who threatened to assassinate President Trump is behind bars.”

It turned out Morales Reyes was framed. He did not write the note. Shortly after Morales Reyes was arrested, investigators learned he neither read nor spoke English.

Once it became clear he likely did not write the note, they asked him who might be trying to hurt him. He could only think of one person, a man named Demetric Scott, who was then being held in Milwaukee County Jail, facing charges for stabbing and robbing Morales Reyes. As recorded jail phone calls later revealed, Scott wrote the threatening letter so Morales Reyes would be deported and his case might be dismissed. Scott has since confessed to framing Morales Reyes. DHS maintains the webpage accusing Morales Reyes of the crime.

When DHS announced they had caught a would-be assassin, law enforcement officials already knew he didn’t write the note, according to lawyers for the Morales family. DHS has still not taken down the public webpage claiming he threatened to assassinate the president. There is only a brief disclaimer explaining that he is no longer under investigation for threats against the president.

His daughter Ana Morales said the whole affair has been “heartbreaking” for her family. Her father can no longer live his life in peace. Anxious and depressed, he is afraid to leave the house, having been cast as a presidential assassin, she said during a press conference organized by the immigrant advocacy organization Voces de la Frontera.

“They knew it was a lie when they said it,” said Attorney Mark Thomsen, who is representing the family in their claim against the federal government. “So we have to ask ourselves, what are we doing that allows this lie to continue? Check it out, folks. These are two young people with the courage to stand up to the biggest government on the planet, the most powerful government on the planet, and say, ‘Do the right thing, America.'”

The Morales family is preparing a lawsuit against DHS and ICE for intentional infliction of emotional distress. They have filed a claim seeking damages. The federal government has six months to respond before they file the suit, Thomsen said. The federal government’s false claims about Morales Reyes kicked off a torrent of harassment against the family, much of it on social media.

“I really think that they knew what they were doing,” his son Antonio Morales said. “They wanted to do this to us. They wanted to do this to more immigrants, and they really want to keep terrorizing the community going forward.”

Morales Reyes has lived in the U.S. since 1986. He was working as a dishwasher at a Chili’s at the time of his arrest and had an open application for a U visa, which is a special visa for immigrants who have been a victim of a crime in the U.S. Since his arrest, the federal government has initiated removal proceedings against him. His immigration attorney, Cain Oulahan, said immigration courts have a massive backlog of U visa cases and it’s unlikely a decision would come before a court decides his deportation case.

“It will probably take around eight years to get a decision on [the U visa],” Oulahan said.

In the meantime, his family is seeking a total of $5.5 million in damages — $1.5 million for Morales Reyes and another $1 million for each of his four family members — for intentional infliction of emotional distress by the federal government.

“We’re asking for the federal government to do the right thing. That’s what we’re asking for,” Thomsen said. “They wanted to crush Ramon and his family as human beings.”

In the claim, filed Aug. 28, attorneys note that President Donald Trump sought damages of $230 million over the federal investigations into him. “It seems only fair that Mr. Morales Reyes and his family should be entitled to $5.5 million total based on DHS altering the course of their lives forever by proliferating the lie of a man who had previously stabbed Mr. Morales Reyes,” Thomsen and Oulahan wrote in the claim.

Emilio De Torre, executive director of the Milwaukee Turners, said the Morales Reyes case represented a clarion call for the community to do what they can to protect democracy and a free society. Christine Neumann-Ortiz, executive director of Voces, said DHS has been conducting a campaign of systematic abuse against immigrants and U.S. citizens across the country, violating constitutional rights, using excessive force and killing.

“We need meaningful accountability in our court system to protect ourselves from the abuses by DHS,” Neumann-Ortiz said. “If we do not force the government to respect our fundamental human rights and our constitutional rights, then anyone and everyone is at risk because of encroaching authoritarianism that is trying to consolidate its power over people and our legal system.”

After all the fear and harassment, and with a difficult legal battle still ahead of them, the Morales children are clinging to the hope they can some day return to a life something like it once was.

“We just want to go back to normal with our dad, to be honest,” Antonio said. “Just being with him, not having to worry about people recognizing us, which is going to be impossible now, I guess.”

The litigation group America First Legal (AFL) has filed a federal lawsuit against the State of California on behalf of conservative independent journalist Nick Shirley. AFL seeks to block the enforcement of AB 2624, popularly known as the "Stop Nick Shirley Act."

Governor Gavin Newsom signed AB 2624 in late August; the law takes effect on Oct. 1, 2027. It expands the state's Safe at Home program to include providers, employees and volunteers of immigration support services who document threats and register. Those who enroll receive an alternate mailing address in public records. Additionally, the law prohibits the publication of their personal information or image online with the intent to incite imminent serious harm or to create a reasonable fear for their safety.

Shirley, who has published videos in which he follows workers at migrant-services organizations and alleges suspected fraud in California and Minnesota, contends that the law was born after he exposed an alleged widespread fraud in immigrant communities in both states.

The lawsuit seeks a ruling that defines the extent to which California can restrict the publication of information about certain organizations without violating the First Amendment.

Why Shirley and America First Legal consider it unconstitutional

America First Legal (AFL), together with attorney John W. Howard, has filed the lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of California against Attorney General Rob Bonta and Secretary of State Shirley Weber.

What's at stake: Safety vs. Freedom of the press

text:
A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to reveal who set up the structure of a controversial $1.8bn “anti-weaponization fund” to recompense victims of so-called political lawfare that was reportedly dropped by the justice department last month.

Ivan Davis, the US magistrate judge for the eastern district of Virginia, issued the order compelling discovery materials from the government as part of a lawsuit brought by the Democracy Forward non-profit on behalf of plaintiffs including a fired prosecutor and a college professor acquitted of assaulting federal agents at a protest against an immigration raid in California.

“Today’s order granting discovery is a significant step in getting to the bottom of the slush fund,” said Aman George, senior counsel at the non-profit. “We will continue to meet the government in court until our investigation is complete and the slush fund is permanently halted.”

Last month, Todd Blanche said the fund he proposed before he was confirmed “is dead”. The US attorney general told Fox News Sunday: “The fund is dead or whatever word you want to use. It never started. So, it’s not as if the fund is coming back.”

Democrats maintain that the proposed fund would have been used to compensate prosecuted and since-pardoned January 6 rioters, among others. Blanche said that Trump “believes the justice department was weaponized against a lot of Americans” under the Biden administration, adding: “It really hurt them financially.”

The proposed compensation scheme was set up as part of the settlement Trump reached with the IRS regarding a lawsuit over the leak of his tax returns. The agreement shielded the president and his family from future tax audits.

In July, another federal judge found that the parties had never truly been in conflict and Trump’s $10bn lawsuit against the IRS had only ever been a pretense for setting up the fund.

“There was never adverseness between the parties; there was never a case or controversy; and there was never a question as to who would prevail,” the US district judge Kathleen Williams said in a ruling, adding that the lawsuit had been brought “for an improper purpose – to gain the imprimatur of judicial legitimacy for a ‘settlement’ that had no viable basis in law or fact”.

The proposed fund drew bipartisan criticism in Washington, including opposition from two Republican senators, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, and it put Blanche’s confirmation for attorney general at risk.

Critics of the program have noted that the document demanded by lawmakers did not include signatories to the initial agreement, suggesting that it could be revived. Blanche has said that “there were never commissioners” in charge of the “payout pot”. But Senate Democrat Cory Booker said the agreement guaranteed “nothing … no guarantees whatsoever that this slush fund still can’t go forward”.

Trump has rued the abandonment of the fund and has not ruled out another avenue to compensation. “It is dead, but you know, I wish it weren’t,” he said of the fund at a cabinet meeting in July. “To be honest with you, I think people were horribly treated, horribly abused.”

text:
The New Mexico congressman is asking DHS to ban the devices in immigration enforcement and provide records on training, testing and deployment

Organ Mountain News report

WASHINGTON - U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez is calling on the Department of Homeland Security to cancel a $16.7 million contract for electric shock gloves intended for use by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents.

Vasquez, D-N.M., sent a letter to DHS seeking an immediate halt to the acquisition and deployment of the devices and a broader ban on their use in immigration enforcement and detention operations.

His office said more than 40 members of Congress joined the letter.

The lawmakers are also asking DHS for information about training and protocols for use of the devices, along with records describing how they were tested before being considered for deployment.

Vasquez’s office identified the device as the G.L.O.V.E., an electric shock system worn on the hand.

“Introducing low-visibility electric shock weapons into our immigration enforcement system is an unacceptable escalation that prioritizes physical intimidation and unaccountable force over human safety and administrative accountability,” Vasquez wrote in the letter.

The letter also cites concerns raised by human-rights and medical organizations about electric shock devices and asks DHS to redirect resources toward oversight and humanitarian standards rather than expanded use of force.

Vasquez has repeatedly pressed DHS and ICE over immigration enforcement practices and detention conditions, including through prior oversight letters and proposed legislation requiring greater disclosure of detention, deportation and deaths-in-custody data.

title: Bay Area lawmakers' bills to combat ICE head to Newsom's desk - San José Spotlight
description:
Several state bills spurred by Silicon Valley lawmakers to keep federal immigration agents accountable and uphold rights for detainees are headed to the governor’s desk.
Two of the largest private prison companies, CoreCivic and The GeoGroup, are the major operators running ICE detention centers.
The companies’ profits have grown as President Donald Trump upped federal immigration enforcement and deportations.
More than 50 people have died in ICE detention centers during Trump’s second administration, the highest level of deaths in at least a decade.
Since 2025, federal immigration officers have shot at least 23 people and killed six during immigration enforcement operations, including three U.S. citizens.
text:
Several state bills spurred by Silicon Valley lawmakers to keep federal immigration agents accountable and uphold rights for detainees are headed to the governor’s desk.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facilities have been rife with alleged human rights violations, with reports of inhumane living conditions, sexual abuse, unsanitary food and inadequate medical care. In response, state lawmakers have stepped up to protect immigrant rights with bills that would tax companies operating detention centers, prevent ICE contractors from receiving state grants or loans and allow the federal agency to be sued for monetary damages and First Amendment rights violations.

Gov. Gavin Newsom has until Sept. 30 to approve or veto the bills, which have already been approved by the state Legislature.

Reining in detention centers

Assemblymembers Alex Lee and Ash Kalra co-authored Assembly Bill 1633, which would tax private companies operating immigration detention centers. Lee represents North San Jose, Milpitas, Fremont, Newark and Sunol, while Kalra represents East San Jose and South County. The bill is led by San Francisco Assemblymember Matt Haney.

If signed by Newsom, private detention center operators would be taxed 25% starting July 1, 2028. The money would be used to fund immigration services.

“ICE and its corporate profiteers are abducting tens of thousands of innocent people and warehousing them in detention camps,” Lee told San José Spotlight.

Two of the largest private prison companies, CoreCivic and The GeoGroup, are the major operators running ICE detention centers. CoreCivic runs two large ICE detentions in California — the nearly 2,000-bed Otay Mesa Detention Center in San Diego County and the 2,560-bed California City Detention Facility in Kern County.

The GeoGroup runs five ICE detention facilities in the state— 1,940 bed Adelanto ICE Processing Center in San Bernardino County, the 750-bed Desert View Annex in San Bernardino County (run alongside the Adelanto facility), the 400-bed Mesa Verde ICE Processing Center in Bakersfield, the 700-bed Central Valley Annex in Kern County and the 700-bed Golden State Annex in Kern County.

The companies’ profits have grown as President Donald Trump upped federal immigration enforcement and deportations. In 2025, CoreCivic racked in $2.2 billion in revenue and The GeoGroup made $2.6 billion.

CoreCivic sold Otay Mesa Detention Center and the California City Detention Facility to the federal government on July 2, according to a recent filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, as reported by AP, with the federal government paying more than $739 million for Otay Mesa and more than $732 million for City Detention.

More than 50 people have died in ICE detention centers during Trump’s second administration, the highest level of deaths in at least a decade. Senate Bill 942 — also known as the Civil Detainee Bill of Rights Act — would give immigrants held in detention rights to humane care, safe living conditions and healthy food. It is co-authored by Kalra and state Sen. Dave Cortese.

In addition, Senate Bill 1367, led by state Sen. Sabrina Cervantes from Riverside, would prevent a city or county from approving land use for the building of a detention center or converting a current building to an ICE facility.

“I’m glad we were able to pass many pieces of important legislation to hold ICE accountable in California and protect vulnerable communities,” Kalra told San José Spotlight. “My committee worked on SB 942, which is the nation’s first Detainee Bill of Rights, and will enforce much-needed safety and dignity standards for those held in immigration detention.”

Keeping agents in check

Multiple bills awaiting Newsom’s signature aim to address how ICE agents have largely acted with impunity during raids and arrests.

Assembly Bill 2760, led by Lee and co-authored by Kalra, would ban federal immigration agents, as well as local and state officers, from wearing electric shock gloves — and police departments from purchasing them. Lawmakers passed the last-minute bill in response to the Trump administration’s announcement last month to spend up to $20 million on the devices.

Senate Bill 873, co-authored by Kalra, aims to prevent arrests by ICE at courthouses. Senate Bill 747, the No Kings Act, led by state Sen. Scott Wiener of San Francisco, will allow people to sue ICE for constitutional violations. Assembly Bill 1806, spearheaded by Southern California Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, would require the state attorney general to investigate killings of unarmed residents by immigration agents.

Since 2025, federal immigration officers have shot at least 23 people and killed six during immigration enforcement operations, including three U.S. citizens.

While mass enforcement actions like the federal deployment in Los Angeles and Minneapolis, Minnesota haven’t occurred in Santa Clara County, the region is one of the most impacted areas for targeted ICE operations, according to the Services, Immigrant Rights and Education Network (SIREN). The organization is part of the Rapid Response Network of Santa Clara County, a group of volunteers that documents ICE activity, sends alerts to residents and provides free emergency legal support for immigrants.

Since the start of 2025 to June 2026, 232 county residents have been detained, according to the network. Fears of ICE have kept San Jose students from attending class and slowed foot traffic at Latino-owned businesses. Some undocumented residents have chosen to self-deport.

Lee also spearheaded Assembly Bill 2465 to ensure ICE contractors such as tech giant Palantir Technologies, which provides the government with data-mining software to track immigrants, do not get government grants or loans. ICE is paying $30 million through 2027 to use Palantir’s platform.

In the second quarter of 2026, Palantir made $809 million from government contracts — 90% more than what it brought in a year ago.

The extent to which California would benefit from the bill is unknown, as the state does not track how many tax credits it gives to contractors.

“We have clients and community members who have endured the terrible conditions in these facilities,” Huy Tran, executive director of SIREN, told San José Spotlight. “This industry is built on heartbreak and AB 1633 and AB 2465 makes it clear that California will not allow immoral profiteering to go unchecked.”

Contact Joyce Chu at joyce@sanjosespotlight.com or @joyce_speaks on X.

Records released by the ACLU of Arizona detail calls between Pima County Sheriff’s Department deputies and the Border Patrol.

That follows a Pima County Superior Court ruling in July that compelled the sheriff’s department to turn the records over.
