Sheriff Chris Nanos has said his department does not work with immigration enforcement, and the department no longer has a policy to keep those records in place.

But the ACLU AZ’s initial lawsuit turned over a trove of documents showing interactions between the two agencies going up to 2024. The group filed an additional brief with the court earlier this year to receive more recent records.

The ACLU says it received more than 1,800 “unsorted incident reports” that contained "Border Patrol" or other terms, and distilled those into documents showing more than 80 different times deputies made contact with the immigration agency during traffic stops or other interactions.

The documents depict a range of incidents, from drug busts and domestic violence calls, to suspicious person calls that don't result in an arrest.

The Pima County Sheriff’s Department said Nanos was not available Friday for comment on the lawsuit, documents or the department's policy on contacting immigration agencies.

text:
The family of Pierre Damas Bel, a 20-year-old Haitian immigrant in Springfield Ohio, says he died by suicide August 31 after losing Temporary Protected Status.

Bel, an avid soccer player and JROTC member, was beginning his freshman year as an honors neuroscience student at Wright State University. But in July, Bel became one of about 340,000 Haitians in the US whose Temporary Protected Status expired, after the Supreme Court ruled not to intervene. In late July, Immigrations and Customs Enforcement fitted Bel with an electronic ankle monitor, one of the ways the agency tracks people who it may soon deport.

As the device interfered with and stigmatized his day-to-day life, Bel’s family says he became withdrawn. “After my son was outfitted with this ankle monitor, he felt like he was treated like an animal,” Bel’s father, Pierre Ronal Bel, wrote in a statement.

Pierre Damas Bel uploaded a picture of the ankle monitor on Instagram in late July. “I came to this country to pursue my education. I didn’t come here to commit a crime or hurt anyone,” he wrote in the caption. “Yet now I’m walking through the streets of the United States with a GPS monitor on my leg, carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation that I never imagined I would experience.”

“I came here to study, to build my future, and to live a better [life] not to be treated like criminal,” he wrote. “So now, how am I supposed play college sports with a GPS monitor on my leg?”

Bel’s next asylum court hearing was scheduled for October. Vilés Dorsainvil, executive director of the Haitian Support Center in Springfield, is working to support the family. As Dorsainvil told Mother Jones in June, deportation to Haiti can be a matter of “life and death.” The State Department maintains a “do not travel” advisory for risk of kidnappings, sexual assault, and robbery in Haiti. Haitians will face the same dangers if deported back, Dorsainvil said: “There is no safe place in Haiti.”

“No one is required to stay in the United States illegally and wear a monitor,” an ICE spokesperson said. “Any attempts to blame ICE for the death of Pierre Damas Bel are false.”

“These policies are what caused his untimely death,” Guerline Jozef of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, an Ohio legal aid nonprofit, told The Washington Post.

Ohio’s Republican governor, Mike DeWine, called Bel’s death a “horrible, horrible tragedy” and said that ending TPS for Haitian residents was “misguided and wrong,” Capital B reported.

text:
KABUL, AFGHANISTAN – Guyana has announced that six migrants from Afghanistan and Cuba arrived in the country after being deported from the United States.

According to an Associated Press Report, Guyana’s Foreign Minister Robert Persaud said the six people arrived on Friday.

Persaud said the Guyanese government reviewed the individuals’ backgrounds and confirmed that none had a criminal record before agreeing to accept them.

The foreign minister said the six migrants were deported from the United States because of issues related to their immigration status.

According to Persaud, Guyana reached an agreement with the United States to host the migrants following months of negotiations.

He said the agreement will remain in effect for one year and does not mean that the migrants will be permanently resettled in Guyana.

Under the arrangement, migrants transferred to Guyana through a government-supported voluntary return program will remain in the country while their immigration status is determined. They could eventually be returned to their countries of origin or transferred to another country, according to the Associated Press.

Guyanese officials said the International Organization for Migration (IOM) is responsible for implementing the program, while the Guyanese government will not bear the costs of housing or supporting the migrants.

Guyana is a small country in northeastern South America and the Caribbean region. It has reached an agreement with the United States to accept some migrants who have been deported from the country.

The United States has been seeking to hold some deported migrants in so-called “return centers” in third countries while their cases are processed. Washington has been negotiating similar arrangements with several countries as part of its broader immigration enforcement efforts.

The move comes amid broader shifts in US immigration and foreign policy under President Donald Trump. Shortly after taking office in January 2025, Trump signed an executive order pausing refugee admissions to the United States, including for Afghans who assisted American forces.

In November 2025, following a shooting in Washington involving an Afghan national who killed a US National Guard member and injured another, Trump ordered a halt to all Afghan settlement programs and visa issuance for Afghan passport holders. He also directed a full review of Afghans admitted to the United States during the Biden administration.

These policy changes affected thousands of Afghans awaiting relocation to the United States from third countries, including former interpreters, contractors, and civil society workers who supported U.S. operations over two decades. Many remain at risk under Taliban rule or are stranded in neighboring countries with limited legal protections.

text:
A federal judge has temporarily blocked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement from removing an Angolan asylum seeker from Maine after federal agents arrested him outside his workplace in Lewiston this week.

Adnero Pinto Sebastiao, an Angolan national with a pending asylum application, was taken into ICE custody Thursday as he returned from lunch to his job at a Lewiston-area bank, according to court filings and published reports.

His attorneys quickly went to federal court, challenging the detention and seeking an emergency order preventing ICE from transferring Sebastiao out of state before a judge could review the circumstances surrounding his arrest.

The court granted that request.

Under the order, the federal government is prohibited from deporting Sebastiao or transferring him to an immigration detention facility outside Maine while the litigation remains pending. The government must also explain the legal basis for holding him.

Sebastiao reportedly entered the United States legally on a tourist visa before applying for asylum. His immigration case remains pending.

The arrest raises an increasingly familiar legal question as the Trump administration expands immigration enforcement across Maine and the rest of New England: whether having a pending asylum claim or other immigration application protects an individual from detention while the underlying case is being decided.

In Sebastiao’s case, at least for now, a federal judge has made sure ICE cannot move him hundreds of miles away while that question is litigated.

The Department of Homeland Security has declined to discuss the specifics of the case, citing pending litigation.

The Lewiston arrest comes amid heightened ICE activity across Maine and growing scrutiny of how and where federal immigration agents are making arrests.

It also bears similarities to another case involving Lewiston resident Eduardo Jose Alves.

Earlier this summer, a federal judge ordered Alves released after ICE transferred him from Maine to a detention facility in Massachusetts despite a court order restricting the government’s ability to move him.

That dispute became another flashpoint between immigration authorities and attorneys challenging the Trump administration’s enforcement tactics.

Immigration advocates have also criticized recent arrests of people who have no reported criminal convictions and who are already navigating the federal immigration system through asylum claims or other applications.

ICE, however, has repeatedly emphasized that being in the country without lawful immigration status can make an individual subject to enforcement regardless of whether that person has a criminal record.

Recent immigration enforcement operations have demonstrated that the administration is not limiting arrests to violent criminals, convicted felons or individuals facing new criminal charges. People with pending immigration proceedings may also find themselves detained while those cases work their way through a system that can take years to resolve.

The Sebastiao case will now test whether ICE had sufficient legal authority to detain him under the specific circumstances of his immigration status and pending asylum claim.

For the moment, the federal court has drawn a clear line: ICE may continue holding Sebastiao while the case is reviewed, but it cannot move him out of Maine or deport him before the court has an opportunity to determine whether his detention is lawful.

The underlying challenge remains pending in federal court.

The Maine Wire will continue following the case as the federal government responds to the court’s order.

text:
The judicial authorities of the United States have given the green light in total to 19 forced feeding procedures for immigrants on hunger strike, who were protesting their detention under the custody of the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The most recent case affects a Cuban citizen detained at the ICE Processing Center in Montgomery, Texas, a facility operated by the private company GEO Group. According to an investigation by the British newspaper 'The Guardian', a court would have allowed a non-consensual surgery to facilitate his forced feeding directly into the stomach.

In these 19 cases registered since January 2025, ICE went to the courts to request an "involuntary medical procedure" in order to impose forced feeding, a practice that human rights advocacy organizations describe as mistreatment and torture.

"The cruelty of ICE to end legitimate protests reaches the extreme of cutting the body of the protester to insert a tube into his stomach. It is an example of the horrors that occur out of our sight in ICE detention centers," denounced the lawyer of the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), Savannah Kumar.

According to the court order signed by federal judge Andrew Hanen of the Southern District of Texas, which 'The Guardian' has accessed, in August a nasogastric tube was placed on the detainee to force-feed him. Now, ICE would have obtained the extension of that order and permission for an additional intervention called "percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy."

The Department of Homeland Security, of which ICE is a part, stated on Thursday that the man had "resumed his feeding" and that he was no longer being force-fed. However, it does not refer to the authorized surgery nor clarify whether he resumed food intake before or after the judicial approval of the operation, which apparently has not yet been carried out.

The British newspaper indicates that it has not released the name of the Cuban because it has not been able to establish contact with him. He was detained on July 22 and declared a hunger strike three days later. He has been residing in the country since 1980 and in 2004 a deportation order was issued against him.

text:
Brian José Morales García was riding beside his boss through the Texas Hill Country, bound for an air-conditioning job near Fredericksburg, when a state trooper stopped their pickup truck.

Over the next four days, the 25-year-old was shuttled through a succession of detention facilities. Along the way, his attorney said, he was stripped, shoved and threatened with years in prison. By April 7, he was aboard a deportation flight to Mexico.

The country sending him away was his own.

Morales García was born in Denver, according to a copy of his birth certificate reviewed by USA TODAY.

He is part of a long, largely uncounted history of U.S. citizens swallowed by the nation’s immigration system. The federal government does not release data on how often its agents detain or deport U.S. citizens, but investigations by journalists, researchers and oversight agencies have documented thousands of citizens detained, deported or otherwise targeted by immigration authorities across decades. One study estimated that U.S. citizens account for as many as 1.5% of all deportees.

A Government Accountability Office report from 2021 offers one glimpse of how often Americans may become entangled in immigration enforcement. Between fiscal year 2015 and the first two quarters of fiscal year 2020, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested 674 potential U.S. citizens, detained 121 and deported 70, according to the report. The majority of those deportations — 66 people — occurred during President Donald Trump’s first term.

Yet, even those numbers do not tell the full story. The watchdog agency found that ICE did not consistently track cases involving potential U.S. citizens, making it impossible to know how many people were actually swept into the system.

The problem has persisted through successive Republican and Democratic administrations. Now, experts fear a persistent failure is colliding with a rapid expansion of immigration enforcement — one pushed to deliver record numbers of arrests, increasingly aided by state and local police and operating with fewer internal checks. The result, they warn, is that more citizens could be swept into the dragnet and have fewer places to turn once they are.

“This is a system that is advancing with less accountability now than before,” said Jacqueline Stevens, a political science professor at Northwestern University and founder of the school’s Deportation Research Clinic. “And less oversight because they’re not producing the records that they should be producing on these cases.”

Citizens represent a sliver of those targeted by immigration authorities. But for those who are wrongfully detained or deported, the experience can leave lasting trauma, mounting legal costs and consequences that take years to resolve.

For Morales García, returning home required a federal lawsuit — and nearly five months outside his own country.

The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to USA TODAY's requests for comment. The Department of Justice declined to comment on Morales García's case, citing pending litigation. In court filings, however, the government said Morales García told federal agents he was born in Mexico and freely chose to return there.

How a traffic stop ended in deportation

In 2001, Morales García was born in Denver to two young Mexican parents who had come to the United States in search of better opportunities. Later that year, he was baptized at St. Therese Catholic Church in Aurora, Colorado, where a baptismal record lists Denver as his birthplace. Morales García also has a Social Security card, a copy of which USA TODAY reviewed. Like cards issued to U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents, his bears no restriction requiring DHS authorization to work.

But the family’s life in the United States was brief. After Morales García’s younger brother was born in 2002, his parents returned to Mexico to raise their sons close to family, said his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch. Morales García would spend most of the next two decades there, growing up speaking Spanish and eventually getting married.

As he prepared to become a father, Morales García returned to the United States to find work and support his growing family in Mexico, including his wife who was pregnant with their first daughter. He drove north from Aguascalientes — a sunbaked city in Mexico’s central highlands — in January 2025. At the port of entry, Morales García showed a U.S. Customs and Border Protection officer his Colorado birth certificate, Lincoln-Goldfinch said. The officer let him through.

He settled in Austin, moving through a series of construction jobs before landing one installing air-conditioning units.

On April 3, he was riding to one of those jobs when Texas Department of Public Safety troopers stopped his employer’s pickup near Fredericksburg for an alleged window tint violation, according to the federal lawsuit his attorneys later filed. No one in the truck received a citation as a result of the stop, Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

Morales García repeatedly told the state troopers — and, later, the Gillespie County sheriff's deputies who were called in to translate — that he is American. He explained in Spanish that he had been born in Denver and asked for an opportunity to retrieve his documents, Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

The officers, however, contacted ICE. The agency instructed them to hold Morales García and another passenger, according to the lawsuit, and Morales García was booked into the Gillespie County Jail. Both Texas DPS and the Gillespie County Sheriff’s Office have formal partnerships with ICE, part of a growing network of state and local agencies enlisted to help enforce federal immigration law.

“There's no law in this country that says that U.S. citizens have to have ID on them when they're going out or riding as passengers in a car,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said. “What's happening in the streets is that DPS, ICE and all the sheriffs are just stopping people with brown skin and asking them what their status is, and if they don't have an answer that they like, they're taking them. And it's quiet and it's silent what they're doing, but it's a slippery slope.”

Morales García was ultimately transferred into CBP custody. There, Lincoln-Goldfinch said, agents ridiculed his repeated claims that he was American and warned that, if he continued making them, he could face as many as five years in prison.

“At that point, he'd been abused for four days straight, and he believed that he was going to either sign the paperwork they told him to sign or go to jail for years,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said. “So he signed these documents... under duress.”

With his signature, Morales García had agreed to be deported to Mexico.

'The 900-pound gorilla in the coal mine'

Morales García’s ordeal fits a pattern Stevens, the political scientist, has spent decades tracing. Some people discover only after they are detained that they have a claim to U.S. citizenship. Others, like Morales García, know they are American from the beginning, yet watch as officers dismiss their claims and the deportation process moves forward anyway.

Stevens calls these cases “the 900-pound gorilla in the coal mine.”

“I study U.S. citizens not because I care more about U.S. citizens being wrongfully deported than anybody else,” she said. “But if even U.S. citizens can’t survive the lawlessness of the deportation process, that tells us a lot about what’s happening to everybody else.”

Claims of citizenship are supposed to interrupt the machinery of deportation. Federal regulations require unresolved claims to be referred to immigration court. ICE policy also requires officers to consult supervisors and attorneys to put their findings in writing. If the evidence suggests the person might be American — even inconclusively — they should be released while the government decides.

Whether those safeguards were followed in Morales García’s case remains unclear.

Still, the 2021 GAO investigation found that the protections were unevenly understood and applied. Some ICE officers had not been trained to follow the agency’s own guidance, and neither ICE nor CBP reliably tracked every citizen that's been detained or removed, the report found. Agents are also not required to correct their databases if someone they investigated turned out to be a citizen.

On paper, it's the government’s job to prove that someone is not a citizen. In reality, Stevens said, the burden often flips — a result, in part, of Supreme Court rulings that have given immigration authorities broad power and few judicial checks, she said.

Yet, what feels different now, Stevens said, is DHS’s growing willingness to double down even after evidence of citizenship emerges.

“Information that’s consistent with deportation is treated as accurate,” she said. “And information that’s inconsistent with deportation is treated as inaccurate and fraudulent.”

Last year, 22-year-old Dulce Consuelo Diaz Morales spent 25 days in ICE custody while DHS challenged her Maryland birth certificate. Months later, she received a U.S. passport, and the government dropped its effort to deport her, the Baltimore Banner reported. In Florida, Juan Carlos Lopez-Gomez, 20, remained jailed even after a judge verified that he was American, while DHS maintained that he had told officers he was undocumented, according to the Oklahoma Voice.

From Mexico, Morales García could do little more than wait while his attorneys tried to reconstruct the paper trail of his life. In May, they filed a federal lawsuit accusing federal, state and local officials of violating his constitutional rights and asking a judge to order the government to bring him home.

Back across the bridge

Three weeks after Morales García’s attorneys sued, the government told a different story.

In a May 21 court filing, Justice Department attorneys said Morales García initially claimed citizenship and told a Border Patrol agent that he had entered the country with a birth certificate. But after the agent warned him that lying could bring criminal charges, they wrote, Morales García stated that he had been born in Zacatecas.

The DOJ denied that he was threatened or coerced, stating in court documents that he freely signed documents requesting a voluntary return to Mexico. It also pointed to Mexican records bearing another birth date, the spelling “Bryan” and an identity code associated with Zacatecas, Mexico.

Lincoln-Goldfinch said Morales García’s mother registered his birth in Mexico in 2004. The registrar, according to the family, entered a different date and changed “Brian” to “Bryan,” a spelling more commonly used there. Having records in two countries — and discrepancies between them — is common among dual citizens, both Lincoln-Goldfinch and Stevens said.

After nearly five months — and a growing file of evidence — the Justice Department agreed to let Morales García return to the United States, Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

On Aug. 30, after a bus ride north from Aguascalientes, Morales García found himself at the border once more. In his hands was the Colorado birth certificate his lawyers had spent months trying to make the government believe. This time, it was enough.

On the other side, his attorneys took him to Starbucks for coffee.

But coming back did not erase what had happened, Morales García said, alleging officers had judged him by how he looked and by the English he could not speak. He worried another traffic stop could end the same way.

“That fear will always be with me,” he said in Spanish during a news conference. “It happened once and it can happen a second time.”

His return did not end the lawsuit. Richard “Dicky” Grigg, one of his attorneys, said they plan to seek damages to keep other citizens from going through the same ordeal.

“They sent this man, a U.S. citizen, to Mexico, took four months of his life and then let him back in the United States when they realized they'd made a mistake,” Grigg said. “To prevent this from happening in the future, we’re going to do what we can to make sure government officials, state and federal, are held accountable and responsible.”

Morales García’s own plans are simpler. He wants to return to work and do what he came to the United States to do in the first place.

“Echarle ganas,” he said — to keep going, keep working and keep giving it his all.

text:
Upper Darby continues efforts limiting federal immigration actions in the town.

After passing a resolution in February stating police will not enforce non-criminal federal immigration laws, the council will now look at changing township codes to place limitations on the use of township resources in aid of civil federal immigration enforcement.

Officials have estimated there have been hundreds of ICE arrests within the township.

Ordinance 2026-12′s stated purpose would limit township personnel assisting civil federal immigration enforcement, safeguard constitutional rights, and promote public safety and trust between the community and local government.

The detailed 17-page ordinance would prohibit the use of township resources to assist U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Among the rules the ordinance outlines include township personnel shall not honor or enforce an immigration detainer or administrative warrant unless accompanied by a valid judicial warrant; immigration status will not be asked or maintained by township employees.

Some of the other points of the ordinance:

• If ICE presents a judicial warrant to a township employee they are required to contact the police superintendent who would contact the township solicitor to confirm the warrant.

• No township official, employee, or agency shall support or assist ICE, and township resources will not be used to provide protection, logistical support, or operational assistance to federal ICE agents engaged in civil immigration enforcement.

• Township property shall not be used as a staging location for any federal immigration enforcement operation conductedby a federal immigration enforcement agency.

• No township equipment such as radios, cellphones, emails or data bases shall be used to provide information to immigration enforcement.

• When there is a lawful custody transfer, nothing prohibits a federal law enforcement or immigration enforcement official from entering upon or temporarily using township property with a valid judicial warrant.

• For ICE agents it requests they clearly identify themselves by name, badge and agency and to refrain from masking or concealing their identities.

The ordinance does have an impact for township police. It would restrict officers from wearing masks in most instances.

• Township officers including the emergency services unit, the narcotics unit and intelligence units should not wear masks or face coverings unless the superintendent or his designee determines it is reasonably necessary for safety, operational security, protection of the officer’s identity or undercover assignments or for safety.

The ordinance states the township will obey valid court orders.

The ordinance would prevent township police from detaining someone based on their immigration status, or because of an ICE administrative warrant or civil detainer.

The ordinance requires training for all township departments on the new policy.

Range of comments

During discussion Council Member At Large Kyle McIntyre said 1 in 4 residents in the township have been born somewhere other than the United States and many live here in fear.

“Our residents are being targeted, having their status ripped away, being denied a day in court, denied a future my ancestors fought and died fleeing Ireland for,” he said.

He said they can’t control what Washington does but they can decide what their government does within their legal authority.

“Officers are here to protect Upper Darby first, that we protect the information residents give us, that we reject 287 (g) agreements,” McIntyre said.

During public comment most residents spoke in favor of the ordinance, including state Sen. Tim Kearney, D-26.

Kearney said calls about ICE actions in Upper Darby are the most frequent topic he gets to his office.

“The ordinance directly addresses many of the concerns directed to my office and demands for clear policies at the local level,” Kearney said. “It respects the rule of law while making it crystal clear … (that) the township will not aid the administration’s cruel and mass deportation campaign.”

Kearney said that similar laws have been introduced in the state Legislature.

One resident said that while she supports the ordinance, “before we want to tell police not to lock somebody up who might be breaking into your house … we have criminals that came in here, too. It’s not all peaches and cream and roses in Upper Darby,” she said. “And they need to be held accountable, too.”

At-large council members Marion Minik and Noah Fields questioned the timing of the resolution, complaining the ordinance didn’t appear on the agenda until the last minute and they hadn’t had time to study it.

President Michelle Billups shut them down, stating the ordinance had gone through two committees with revisions going back and forth with the solicitor and with Police Superintendent Timothy Bernhardt.

Council member Melissa DiNofia-Bozzone asked if a public safety committee could hold a hearing on the issue before the next council meeting and was told that would happen.

In the end, the vote was unanimous for a resolution to be on the agenda for the Sept. 16 council meeting.

The quick ticket system

The recent meeting also included final approval of the proposed Licenses and Inspections quick ticket system for 17 quality-of-life issues.

Amrinder Singh, director of Licenses & Inspections, patiently answered most questions on the 17 property maintenance and quality-of-life violations that could result in fines of $50 to $100.

One resident asked about pollinator-friendly gardens and the idea that we have to have everything short and edged saying, “We are not neglecting our yards,” while another resident complained his neighbor was “breaking and cutting down a goat” that was bleeding all over his stairwell. He said he contacted multiple officials and nobody wanted to touch that issue.

One resident said a fine shouldn’t be the first step and worried about weaponization of the system.

The ticket system passed unanimously.

Fire stations issue

Council members McNelly and Fields brought up the question on eminent domain and the township fire stations. McNelly asked about negotiations on the purchase of Highland Park Fire Company.

Chief Administrative Officer Crandell Jones said the township is putting together appraisals and a matrix on the implications about all five firehouses, whether that be rental or purchase. He said they are awaiting two appraisals.

Fields asked if they are authorizing payments or reimbursements on mortgage payments.

He was told that the township only filed a declaration of taking on the fire station on West Chester Pike, and are in negotiations. The others are being reviewed and legitimate expenses are being reimbursed.

Guyana’s Foreign Secretary Robert Persaud said the six people arrived on Saturday after being vetted and found to have no criminal backgrounds.

“The US has not made any further requests” for non-citizen deportations to be sent to Guyana at this time, Persaud told The Associated Press news agency.

Persaud said Guyana agreed to receive the deportees after months of negotiations.

The one-year arrangement does not constitute permanent resettlement, he said.

The latest deportations are part of the Trump administration’s broader campaign to remove migrants from the United States, including through arrangements that send foreign nationals to countries other than their countries of origin.

More than 30 countries have entered such agreements with the United States since Trump returned to office, according to Amnesty International, including 15 countries in the Americas.

Third-country deportations can send people to countries they have never lived in, where they may have no familiarity with local conditions or language.

The Trump administration has expanded such arrangements with governments around the world, including several in Africa, with some agreements involving multimillion-dollar payments.

US officials have defended the policy by arguing that countries such as Cuba refuse to accept deportees from the United States.

Rights groups, however, have condemned the practice as a means of punishing migrants and pressuring them to abandon their immigration claims in the United States.

Many people subjected to the deportations have no criminal background.

The Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse (TRAC), a research organisation at Syracuse University, estimates that 70.6 percent of foreign nationals currently in US immigration detention have no criminal conviction.

The policy has also raised concerns over the conditions awaiting deportees in countries facing poverty, instability, conflict or human rights abuses.

The six people sent to Guyana will receive assistance through the Assisted Voluntary Return Programme, run by the United Nations International Organisation for Migration (IOM).

Under the arrangement, they will remain in Guyana while their immigration cases are determined.

They could eventually return to their countries of origin or seek relocation elsewhere.

The Trump administration has also cancelled immigration protections, including programmes such as Temporary Protected Status and humanitarian parole, leaving tens of thousands of migrants exposed to deportation.

Reports have also emerged that the administration plans to strip visas from roughly 200,000 people seeking asylum.

The removal of legal immigration status can expose migrants to deportation even when conflicts or unstable conditions remain in their countries of origin.

On the morning of April 18, Agustin Ramirez Reyna was pulled over by a Franklin County sheriff’s deputy and charged with failing to have his vehicle inspected.

Long before the traffic infraction was dismissed two months later, it had been overshadowed by a more serious allegation: Ramirez Reyna was not a legal citizen of the United States.

He is now facing deportation.

The Mexican native’s apprehension was part of a federal program that allows local law enforcement officers to act as agents of Immigration and Customs Enforcement — a practice that a judge let stand last week while a legal battle plays out.

How local law enforcement coordinates with ICE

The U.S. Department of Justice is challenging a law passed earlier this year by Virginia’s General Assembly that places restrictions on the voluntary contracts between ICE and law enforcement agencies, known as 287(g) agreements.

Ruling that DOJ will likely prevail in its lawsuit, U.S. District Judge Robert Payne granted the government’s request for a preliminary injunction that forestalled provisions that would have taken effect Sept. 1.

The ruling means that arrests like Ramirez Reyna’s will likely continue.

“The Franklin County Sheriff’s Office remains an active participant in the 287(g) program,” Sgt. Megan Huston wrote in a recent email to The Roanoke Times.

Over the past year, about 55 undocumented immigrants have been stopped for traffic offenses in the county and then turned over to ICE, which in turn has transferred them to an immigrant detention center to face deportation hearings, according to documents obtained through open-record requests.

Twenty-six sheriff’s offices and police departments in Virginia have opted to join the 287(g) program, Payne wrote in his opinion. The Franklin County Sheriff’s Office is the only one in the Roanoke and New River valleys, after Craig County withdrew from its agreement earlier this year.

About a half-dozen deputies were certified to make arrests after receiving training from ICE. Their immigration work is usually performed during their on-duty hours with the county.

Although arrests by state authorities represent an infinitely tiny fraction of ICE’s nationwide total — President Donald Trump has set a goal of 2,000 arrests per day as part of his immigration crackdown — critics say the program diverts resources away from the primary mission of local law enforcement.

“We are very concerned that existing 287(g) agreements will be allowed to continue,” the Legal Aid Justice Center, a Charlottesville-based nonprofit with a mission that includes advocating for immigrants, said in a statement following Payne’s decision.

“These agreements entangle local law enforcement in federal immigration enforcement, which undermines the trust communities need to report crimes and cooperate with investigations,” the statement read.

Who is Ramirez Reyna?

The story of how Agustin Ramirez Reyna came to America — and how he may be forced to return to Mexico — is detailed in court papers filed by the Legal Aid Justice Center.

In early 2023, he made his way into the country to find a better life and an income that let him send money back to his mother.

After crossing the border without encountering immigration officials, he eventually came to live in Rocky Mount, where he found work as a roofer.

Ramirez Reyna, 36, began dating a woman who is a U.S. citizen. They were married in October 2023, and two years later had a son. Earlier this year, he began the process of adjusting his status as an immigrant through his marriage.

On the morning of April 18, he was driving with his family to visit friends when he passed a sheriff’s deputy’s car heading in the other direction on Scuffling Hill Road.

The sheriff’s deputy made a U-turn and followed Ramirez Reyna to his friend’s house before activating his flashing lights and informing him that he was being stopped for having expired inspection stickers.

“The officer then asked Mr. Ramirez Reyna if he was legal or illegal,” Alex Kornya, an attorney with the Legal Aid Justice Center who represents him, would later write in court papers. “His wife told the officer that they were in the process of adjusting his status.”

After making a call to an ICE official who confirmed that Ramirez Reyna was in the country illegally, the deputy paced him in handcuffs and took him to the Western Virginia Regional Jail.

Although Ramirez Reyna had no criminal record, Kornya wrote in court records, he was then transferred to an immigration detention center in Farmville, where he was held without bond to face deportation.

Immigrants like Ramirez Reyna had long been considered eligible for bond pending their hearings in immigration court, Kornya said.

“Then the new administration, roughly a year ago, did this 180-degree turn and by recharacterizing some definitions under the Immigration and Nationality Act, effectively denied almost anyone who would be subject to detention the opportunity for bond,” the attorney said in a recent interview.

Virginia sought to void the contracts unless, in exchange, it could control the operations of ICE agents within its borders, the lawsuit stated.

“Such a bargain is no bargain at all, and the law demanding it is unconstitutional,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Gerard Mene wrote in the 47-page filing.

Before granting DOJ’s request for a preliminary injunction, which puts the law on hold pending a trial, Payne was required to find that the federal government was likely to win on the merits of its lawsuit.

The judge did so in an opinion filed Thursday in Richmond’s federal court.

“States are not entitled to themselves control or regulate the federal enforcement of laws, no matter how strongly (or rightly) they disagree with the means the government uses to enforce federal law,” Payne wrote.

“In other words, what would become of a dual system of sovereignty if States were free to do as Virginia has done here?” his opinion concluded.

“No doubt, it would endure, but, without doubt, it would be altered.”

title: A student, detained. A husband, deported. Reasons Hoosiers protest ICE - IndyStar
description:
The crowd chanted: "ICE, ICE, go away!
Then one of her students called her from the ICE building: "Hey.
Before the protest, Franklin sat in the grass with Emmanuel to draw her sign.
Music blared from a speaker in the parking lot, where a few participants sat in lawn chairs and wrote messages on posters.
Across the street, the ICE building remained still and silent.
text:
More than 130 people gathered in a parking lot across from the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement building on Woodland Drive on Sept. 5, protesting the agency's presence after a wave of detentions in Indianapolis last week.

Participants lined up at the edge of Woodland Drive, waving signs and blowing a chorus of whistles. A smaller group held up posters on the other side of the lot, facing Interstate 465. The crowd chanted: "ICE, ICE, go away! Immigrants are here to stay!"

The temperature was 86 degrees and rising, and the sun beat down on the sea of parking lots, warehouses, and squat, dark-windowed offices around the ICE building. But protest organizers were undeterred, passing out water bottles, granola bars and more whistles.

The two women who convened the demonstration, Helene Rodriguez and Josselyn Reyes, said they had never organized a protest before — until Sept. 5, when they donned neon safety vests and took up megaphones. Rodriguez and Reyes are longtime friends and have both worked in immigration law offices, though Rodriguez is now an English as a Second Language teacher.

The friends knew they had to do something after the latest wave of ICE actions, Rodriguez said. She first saw posts about the Indianapolis raids on Facebook. Then one of her students called her from the ICE building: "Hey. I just got detained by ICE," he told her.

The student is now being held in Clay County Jail, according to Rodriguez. He has a work permit and was on track to graduate from high school soon, she said.

Reyes said she wants to demand due process for immigrants who have been detained suddenly, urged to sign deportation papers, and blocked from consulting attorneys.

"We are here because we believe every person deserves dignity and humanity," she said.

Once Rodriguez and Reyes began publicizing the protest, Indianapolis-area chapters of Indivisible, a progressive activist group founded in the wake of President Donald Trump's first election, sent volunteers to help with safety and supplies.

Attendee Melody Franklin brought her 1-year-old son, Emmanuel De Souza. For Franklin, the anti-ICE protest was personal: her husband, Emmanuel's father, was deported to Brazil several years ago under the Biden administration.

Franklin saved up to visit her husband in Brazil, where she spent several months before Emmanuel was born. Now she owns a small spray-tan business downtown and works two other jobs to support her son.

Before the protest, Franklin sat in the grass with Emmanuel to draw her sign. "A boy needs his dad," it read.

Jayla Garcia said she attended the protest to speak up for immigrants like her own family.

"What our parents did for us, they brought us to hustle," Garcia said. "So we've gotta hustle for them."

Nathaly Suarez, 21, and her sister Lesly, 16, joined the protest to defend people they care about who are undocumented — including their parents. Their parents have lived in the U.S. for 20 years, Nathaly said, and have worked hard to provide their children with a better life.

Lesly, a North Central High School student, said she struggles to understand how people can ignore ICE's actions toward immigrants — sudden detainments, lack of access to due process, and even deaths at the hands of immigration officers.

"It's just not fair," Lesly said. "All these people, they fuel our community, they do the work that other people didn't want to."

She knows what she wants to do after she graduates: become an immigration lawyer.

Attendee Hailey Zuercher said she showed up to call for "empathy and human decency."

"At this point, it doesn't really matter what political side you're on," she said. "You need to stand up for people's rights who can't necessarily stand up for themselves. They're scared to come outside, they're scared to go to the grocery store. So if you're able to say something, use your voice."

Cars honked in support as they drove past the demonstration. Music blared from a speaker in the parking lot, where a few participants sat in lawn chairs and wrote messages on posters. Across the street, the ICE building remained still and silent.

Tilly Robinson is a Pulliam Fellow for the Indianapolis Star. She can be reached at tilly.robinson@indystar.com.

description:
Guyana has received six people deported from the United States as the administration of President Donald Trump expands its use of so-called third-country deportations.
Guyana’s Foreign Secretary Robert Persaud said the group of Cuban and Afghan nationals arrived on Saturday after being deported over immigration issues.
Third-country deportations involve sending foreign nationals to countries other than their own.
The Trump administration has expanded the practice, reaching agreements with countries in several regions, some involving multimillion-dollar payments.
Rights groups have condemned third-country deportations as a way of punishing migrants and pressuring them to abandon immigration claims.
text:
Guyana has received six people deported from the United States as the administration of President Donald Trump expands its use of so-called third-country deportations.

Guyana’s Foreign Secretary Robert Persaud said the group of Cuban and Afghan nationals arrived on Saturday after being deported over immigration issues.

“The US has not made any further requests” for non-citizens to be sent to Guyana, Persaud told The Associated Press.

None of the six had criminal backgrounds, he said.

Persaud said Guyana reached an agreement with the US after months of negotiations. The deal will run for one year and does not constitute permanent resettlement.

Third-country deportations involve sending foreign nationals to countries other than their own. Critics say deportees may have no ties to the countries they are sent to and can face unfamiliar languages and difficult conditions.

The Trump administration has expanded the practice, reaching agreements with countries in several regions, some involving multimillion-dollar payments. US officials have defended the policy by arguing that some countries, including Cuba, refuse to accept deportees.

Amnesty International estimates that more than 30 countries have entered such agreements since Trump returned to office, including 15 in the Americas.

Rights groups have condemned third-country deportations as a way of punishing migrants and pressuring them to abandon immigration claims. The practice has also raised concerns over human rights and conditions in countries receiving deportees.

The Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse at Syracuse University estimates that 70.6% of foreign nationals currently held in US immigration detention have no criminal conviction.

The six deportees sent to Guyana will receive assistance through the Assisted Voluntary Return Programme operated by the UN International Organization for Migration. They will remain in Guyana while their immigration cases are resolved and could eventually return to their countries of origin or seek relocation elsewhere.

Restricting immigration and deporting foreign nationals have become central features of Trump’s second-term policies. His administration has also cancelled programmes including Temporary Protected Status and humanitarian parole, leaving tens of thousands at greater risk of deportation.

Reports have also indicated that the administration plans to revoke visas for about 200,000 asylum seekers.

title: Exclusive: Inside the fevered fight to free an East Bay man from ICE detention
description:
They told him he would be taken to the Central Valley Annex, an ICE detention center in McFarland (Kern County) six hours away.
Back at the airport, Estefani had called a rapid response network and then drove to San Francisco.

They drove him back to San Francisco on Wednesday to put him on a flight to Tacoma.
At Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, Chaparro found himself looking over his shoulder, checking for ICE agents, wondering whether they would stop him again.
text:
Sergio Chaparro had just cleared security at Oakland International Airport on the morning of Aug. 28 and was thinking about a preflight coffee when Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents stopped him. They had a warrant for his arrest, they said, and demanded to know his immigration status.

Chaparro and his girlfriend had planned to fly to Las Vegas to celebrate their first anniversary.

“I was excited,” Chaparro said. “I was about to ask Estefani what she wanted for breakfast, and then, boom, the nightmare starts.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Agents shackled the 47-year-old Richmond man and whisked him to a truck waiting outside to take him to ICE’s regional headquarters in downtown San Francisco.

Over the next week, Chaparro pingponged between four ICE offices and detention centers in California and Washington state as his friends and family scrambled to get him access to needed medical care, prevent his deportation and free him.

“I thought it might be a bad idea,” Chaparro said of the Vegas trip as he sat in a park in Point Richmond on Saturday, the day after being freed from ICE custody. “But I’d heard stories from other people who’d done it that nothing happened to them … but I had bad luck.

“I was so scared,” he continued. “I was shaking.”

ICE’s arrest report shows that agents received a referral from the Transportation Security Administration for visa overstay. The arrest came amid a surge of airport arrests by ICE of foreign citizens with expired travel visas, who have traditionally not been targets for deportation. In Chaparro’s case, the government acknowledged that he did not have a criminal history but said he overstayed a tourist visa after entering the U.S. in August 2019.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

ICE officials did not respond to a request for comment Saturday afternoon. They previously told reporters that Chaparro entered the U.S. legally in August 2019, overstayed his visa and remained in the country illegally since then, and would stay in ICE’s custody until he went through removal proceedings.

After Chaparro was taken to ICE’s downtown offices at 630 Sansome St., he said, the officers who detained him showed him some papers they said he needed to sign.

“I’m not going to sign anything without a lawyer present,” Chaparro recalled answering. They told him he would be taken to the Central Valley Annex, an ICE detention center in McFarland (Kern County) six hours away.

But Chaparro, a restaurant manager and father of two young boys, had severe sleep apnea and needed a device called a CPAP machine to help him breathe while he slept. Without it, he could suffocate or have a heart attack.

Back at the airport, Estefani had called a rapid response network and then drove to San Francisco. The next day, she drove down to the Central Valley Annex and called the facility more than a dozen times as staff told her they had to get authorization to accept the equipment.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“I had to call the detention center so many times to follow up,” she said. “This is a serious matter. He needs the machine.”

Chaparro was put in a room with stacked bunk beds — and no power outlets.

“You don’t understand,” Chaparro recalled telling them. “If I don’t use my machine, my life is at risk.”

Detention officers ultimately told him to sleep in the room where new detainees are processed, he said.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

On Monday, while Estefani was visiting Chaparro at the detention center, the facility’s staff told him he was being transferred to another location. They drove him to the Mesa Verde Processing Center in Bakersfield, but were turned away because the facility was full, he said.

ICE returned him to McFarland, where he reentered the facility, a process that took more than six hours, he said.

The next day, he said, ICE agents told him they planned instead to transfer him to the Tacoma Northwest Processing Center in Washington. They drove him back to San Francisco on Wednesday to put him on a flight to Tacoma.

“I was scared,” he said. “I didn’t know anything about Washington. I didn’t know if it was a good location, or a bad one. I didn’t know anything.”

Back in the Bay Area, Chaparro’s case had received significant public attention, and on Wednesday Chaparro’s colleagues at the Oceanview Diner in Berkeley contacted the Alameda County Immigration Legal and Education Partnership, the county’s rapid response network.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“He had such a strong presence and following with staff,” said Will Bishop, co-owner of the diner, which hired Chaparro six years ago. “People would come to the diner in the morning just to see Sergio. … He was a natural leader and people just wanted to be around him.”

When attorneys accepted the case, they learned that Chaparro was sitting in ICE’s San Francisco’s offices waiting to be taken to the airport out of the jurisdiction of the Northern District of California, which immigration attorney Nikolas De Bremaeker said would make securing his release much more difficult.

“We had to, within minutes, file something,” De Bremaeker said. “Normally these are filings that we want to work at least several hours on, to properly review everything.”

De Bremaeker and his colleague, Jazmin Preciado, called ICE’s downtown office repeatedly trying to speak to Chaparro, only to be told that he was already en route to the airport.

“They moved him to the airport shortly after we had started asking to meet with him, which was very striking,” De Bremaeker said. “We needed to speak with him for his representation, and we were denied the chance to do that. … It felt intentional, that they were keeping our client away from us.”

After filing a habeas petition, a formal request for a court review of his detention, the two lawyers then sought a temporary restraining order, filing it early Thursday.

The two lawyers argued in legal filings that ICE had violated Chaparro’s due process rights by not holding a hearing in which they explained why they wanted to detain him.

In Chaparro’s case, De Bremaeker said, he didn’t have a criminal history and the government had never previously targeted him for deportation.

“Folks in this situation have certain due process rights that need to be met, and they were violated by ICE,” he said.

In court documents, federal attorneys argued that the law did not need to provide any hearings in advance of Chaparro’s arrest and said he had “ample” administrative options to protest his detention.

On Friday, however, U.S. District Judge Charles Breyer ruled that Chaparro should be released immediately and barred ICE from re-arresting him before he is able to challenge his detention.

Breyer noted that detention before a removal proceeding is “only justified where immigrants pose flight risks or dangers to the community.”

Chaparro, Breyer said, showed “continuous and long-term residency in the area, sustained employment, local ties, and both minor children and a partner who live in the community,” and “had no criminal record, either in the United States or elsewhere.”

De Bremaeker, who lives in Berkeley, rushed over to the Oceanview Diner to give Chaparro’s colleagues the news.

“Everyone was overjoyed,” said Bishop, the co-owner. “I didn’t realize how stressed out and how down everyone in the restaurant was, how much we had internalized what was happening.” When they learned the news, “everyone, including the customers, cheered. Everyone felt a lot lighter.”

About 720 miles north of San Francisco, ICE officers released Chaparro from the Northwest Processing Center to the street a few hours later Friday, without his drivers license or a way home. He ended up buying a ticket back to San Francisco on Alaska Airlines using documents ICE provided him that confirmed his identity and allowed him to travel back to the Bay Area.

At Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, Chaparro found himself looking over his shoulder, checking for ICE agents, wondering whether they would stop him again.

“It was so, so scary, so weird,” he said. “This is a joke.”

Chaparro landed at San Francisco International Airport shortly before midnight. His girlfriend was waiting for him inside the airport. They hugged, through tears, for what seemed like five minutes.

title: Santa Cruz County immigration arrests steadily increase as nationwide arrests surge
description:
At least four arrests this year Santa Cruz Local identified seven arrests in Santa Cruz County over the past two years in federal data.
Santa Cruz Local is requesting and compiling documentation of these “courtesy notices” in Santa Cruz County on an ongoing basis.
See notices provided to Santa Cruz Police, Watsonville Police, and the Santa Cruz County Sheriff’s Office.
The Santa Cruz County Office of the Public Defender assists non-citizens who pled guilty or no-contest without fully understanding their sentence.
Nonprofits that provide immigration legal assistance include Santa Cruz County Immigration Project: Catholic Charities, Watsonville Law Center, and Latinan.
text:
At least four arrests this year

Santa Cruz Local identified seven arrests in Santa Cruz County over the past two years in federal data. Additional arrests may have occurred if federal agents did not clearly document their location. Numerous arrests in the data are missing location information.

Across Northern California, ICE has increasingly targeted people without a criminal record. But in Santa Cruz County, most documented arrests have been of people with charges or past convictions.

An ICE spokesman shared details about two recent cases but declined to elaborate on the details of all cases identified by Santa Cruz Local, or to confirm the total number of arrests in Santa Cruz County since 2025.

On Aug. 5, ICE agents arrested 29-year-old Mexican national Martin Sebastian Cruz Diaz in Watsonville, ICE spokesperson Jason Sweeney wrote in a Sept. 4 statement. After years in jail, he was convicted in February of numerous charges, including lewd and lascivious acts with a child aged 14 or 15, and released later that month on time served.

Three people arrested in the county had criminal convictions, and two had pending charges, according to the federal data. One person was documented as having violated only immigration law, and another as having outstanding charges in another country.

One of the two without a criminal record in the U.S. is 64-year-old Canadian national Charles Peter Billone, arrested July 29, who officials said had an arrest warrant in Canada for sexual assault and sexual contact with a child under 14.

One arrest on April 15, 2025, took place at the Santa Cruz County Jail as part of the Criminal Alien Program, a federal effort to arrest people in the country illegally as they leave jail or prison for other offenses.

Ashley Keene, a spokesperson for the Sheriff’s Office, wrote in an Aug. 31 email that their office had no knowledge of the arrest at the jail.

“We do not participate in nor do we coordinate with ICE regarding immigration enforcement actions,” she wrote. “ICE being able to take someone into custody at or near the jail does not mean our agency transferred the person to ICE or cooperated with ICE’s immigration enforcement.”

Phil Neff, lead analyst for the Deportation Data Project, confirmed in an email that not all arrests through the Criminal Alien Program involve collaboration with local law enforcement. This is in part because immigration officials can use jail information shared with the Federal Bureau of Investigation and publicly available jail and court records, to locate and arrest non-citizens leaving jails.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection, or CBP, can also arrest people for immigration-related charges. Increasingly, CBP has carried out arrests far from the borderlands. As border crossings dropped precipitously at the start of Trump’s second term, CBP, which includes border patrol, has had more capacity to conduct enforcement in the interior and to support ICE.

The CBP data obtained by the Deportation Data Project includes the date and time of those arrests, but not the location — meaning the agency may have also arrested people in Santa Cruz County.

An arrest reported by Lookout Santa Cruz alleged to have occurred on Jan. 18, 2025 was not identifiable in ICE, CBP or detention center data. A CBP spokesperson said there was no record of the arrest. Santa Cruz Local was not able to independently verify the arrest and did not include it in our data analysis.

Santa Cruz County Public Defender Heather Rodgers has called for more funding for immigration attorneys in her office to assist residents and expand the services it provides. (Amaya Edwards — Santa Cruz Local/CatchLight Local file)

Notifications to local law enforcement have slowed

Federal immigration agents often notify local law enforcement of their presence ahead of time. Santa Cruz Local is requesting and compiling documentation of these “courtesy notices” in Santa Cruz County on an ongoing basis.

Notices to local law enforcement have decreased since a high of five visits in January, with one visit a month reported in June, July and August. It’s unclear how many visits have been made without informing local law enforcement. For example, there is no record of federal authorities notifying Watsonville Police Department ahead of the Aug. 5 arrest.

See notices provided to Santa Cruz Police, Watsonville Police, and the Santa Cruz County Sheriff’s Office. Scotts Valley Police and Capitola Police reported no notices from federal immigration authorities in the past two years.

Arrests nationally and regionally are increasing

Across the San Francisco Area of Responsibility, which includes Northern California, Hawaii, Guam and the Saipan, arrests have sharply increased over the past six months.

The city with the most arrests since January 2025 — 2,481 — is San Francisco, where an immigration court has been the site of more than 140 courthouse arrests and more than 500 people were arrested during immigration appointments at an ICE field office. Some of those arrested could have been Santa Cruz County residents because San Francisco and Concord are the closest immigration courts.

Other cities with the most arrests include Fresno, Bakersfield, Sacramento and Stockton.

Officials are increasingly not taking people into detention after they are arrested, possibly a sign that other means, including ankle monitors, are being used to monitor arrestees awaiting a court date. That doesn’t appear to be the case for any of the documented arrests in Santa Cruz County.

And although nearly all the people arrested in Santa Cruz County had current or pending criminal charges, an increasing number of people in Northern California have been arrested with no criminal record.

Legal resources for immigrants

Some criminal sentences can bar non-citizens from pursuing legal status, or otherwise place them at a higher risk of deportation. Some people with these sentences may be able to retroactively remove the parts that impact immigration pathways.

The Santa Cruz County Office of the Public Defender assists non-citizens who pled guilty or no-contest without fully understanding their sentence. Often, people plead guilty, “not understanding that it was going to be devastating to their immigration pathways,” said Public Defender Heather Rodgers, “which in turn could impact their ability, especially in this administration, to stay with their families and to raise their children and continue on with their life in this country.”

Public defenders petition the District Attorney to remove or substitute immigration-related penalties. “We have a very high success rate on those petitions,” she said.

In some cases, the public defender’s office may be able to dismiss charges, expunge or seal criminal records, or obtain a vacatur that essentially erases the conviction.

There’s no guarantee that any of these measures will decrease someone’s likelihood of arrest or detention. “At times during this administration, things have felt a little arbitrary,” Rodgers said.

People with pending criminal charges should seek attorneys in both criminal and immigration court, Rodgers said. The Public Defender’s office represents those who cannot afford a private attorney in criminal court, but does not work in immigration court.

Nonprofits that provide immigration legal assistance include Santa Cruz County Immigration Project: Catholic Charities, Watsonville Law Center, and Latinan.

For a private immigration lawyer, Rodgers suggests relying on referrals from a trusted source, like nonprofit legal agencies or the Lawyer Referral Service of Santa Cruz County. Scams are common, especially on social media like Facebook. Notaries are not authorized to provide legal services.

Read more about immigrant rights, making an emergency plan for arrest and other resources.

title: A cartel tortured Julio: The US denied his family asylum and wants to send them to a third country
description:
“I can’t get out of here,” Blanca Hernández recalls her son saying, when he confessed that organized crime had recruited him.
“They want to send us to Ecuador, but it’s worse than Mexico,” says Alondra De Ávila, Julio’s younger sister.
She says Julio was forced to work for a cartel, and that there came a point when a hitman accompanied him everywhere.
Only a year ago, this family laments, the Jalisco State Attorney General’s Office issued its first missing person report for Julio.
But on April 13, 2026, the family received a devastating blow: an immigration judge granted the government’s request to close their asylum application and denied them protections against deportation.
text:
Julio thought that he had found his dream job. He was a driver for a wealthy family in Guadalajara, Mexico’s second-largest city.

At first, his tasks were simple: taking his employer to the beauty salon, shopping, or for tea with her friends. He dropped her children off at school and then took them to their English, piano and swimming lessons. But everything changed when he discovered that they were the wife and children of a drug trafficker. “I can’t get out of here,” Blanca Hernández recalls her son saying, when he confessed that organized crime had recruited him. “The boss has already started asking me to deliver packages,” he told her, horrified, back in 2016.

Ten years later, Julio Alfredo De Ávila Hernández is missing. And several of his relatives now live in the United States: they fled the state of Jalisco without imagining that, by seeking asylum, they would enter a legal labyrinth. Their case has become intertwined with the Trump administration’s harsh immigration policies, which mandate the transfer of asylum seekers to third countries deemed “safe.” This is in order to avoid forcing them to return to their countries of origin, where their lives would be in danger.

In April of 2026, an immigration judge presented options to Julio’s parents and siblings: they could continue their asylum process in Ecuador, Honduras, or Guatemala (in that order). They’ve since initiated an appeal process to try to remain in the United States. “They want to send us to Ecuador, but it’s worse than Mexico,” says Alondra De Ávila, Julio’s younger sister.

Back in 2024, she crossed the border with her son — now four years old — to surrender to immigration authorities and tell her story. “We want to stay here. I don’t want my son to experience what I went through,” the 26-year-old pleads.

Julio’s life in Mexico’s criminal underworld

The day Julio accepted the first package his boss handed him, he knew there would be more to come. When he refused to carry out one of the assignments, the threat was immediate. “He told me that, if I quit working for him, he would kill my family, my wife and my children,” recalls Blanca Hernández, 59, describing a conversation she had with her son.

She says Julio was forced to work for a cartel, and that there came a point when a hitman accompanied him everywhere. They knew where he lived, who his relatives were and what his daily routines looked like. By that point, Julio had no way out.

“He saw them making the cocaine bricks. At parties, my son said, instead of putting out bottles [of alcohol], they would put out a tray with just lines [of cocaine]. They started forcing him to do drugs. If he didn’t want to, they pulled out guns. My son started becoming addicted to drugs,” his mother recounts. “He told me that he had stopped visiting us for our own good, so as not to involve us in his life.”

Blanca’s fears came to pass in the early hours of April 5, 2017. Julio was 31 at the time. A phone call alerted her that something had happened at her son’s home in Tlajomulco de Zúñiga, 20 miles south of Guadalajara. When she arrived, she found a heartbreaking scene. “There were pieces of flesh, already dried. I believe they were my son’s. There was a lot of blood in both bedrooms and in the kitchen. I had never seen so much blood,” she recounts.

Some witnesses told her that, hours earlier, armed men had arrived, wearing what appeared to be police badges. They were traveling in two pickup trucks. “They took out a person [from the house], wrapped in a blanket. It looked like a dead body. They threw him in the truck. Then, they took out a woman and, finally, my son, covered in blood, semi-conscious,” she says.

The family sprang into action. They filed a complaint with the Jalisco Attorney General’s Office, called everyone they knew, plastered Julio’s photograph around the city, spoke to the media and even offered a reward for information that might help locate him. But their efforts had an unexpected consequence: they angered the cartel. Vehicles carrying hooded men armed with assault rifles began following them. Then came direct threats, first through anonymous phone calls.

“They told me that they were the ones who had taken Julio and that they wanted me to hand over what Julio owed them,” reads the statement that Blanca Hernández gave to the Jalisco State Police’s Investigative Division. “If I didn’t, they said that they would cut off my head,” she continues.

Two weeks after Julio’s disappearance, one of his sisters received a video call: she saw her brother being tortured.

“He was covered in blood. They had him tied up. They pulled his hair to lift up his head. My son was covered in bruises. His face was swollen from the punches and covered in blood. His white tank top was completely red with blood,” his mother describes.

That was the last time the family saw him alive. Some time later, a video began circulating on El Blog del Narco, a website that publishes uncensored content related to organized crime in Mexico, showing a horrific act. This is how Jéssica, Julio’s younger sister, describes it: “They were cutting off his hand, from the wrist down. The police in Mexico showed us that video.” The family was able to identify him by a tattoo with his daughter’s name on one of his forearms.

Persecution in Mexico

The cartel made it clear that its threats were serious when several gunmen showed up at the family’s home. They pounded on the door and demanded that Julio’s mother hand over “what Julio had left behind,” according to her statement to investigators. “I couldn’t even speak; I was so scared,” she recounted.

The harassment soon spread to their workplaces and the streets of their neighborhood. One afternoon, the gunmen did not even hesitate to approach two of Julio’s sisters as they were accompanied by small children. “We grabbed the baby from the stroller and ran,” Alondra De Ávila recalls. “When we got home, we locked everything up. We put the sofas in the doorways.”

As soon as they had the chance, they fled to the Guadalajara airport, considering it to be the safest place in the city. Thus began a long journey, passing through the homes of relatives in the states of Jalisco, Aguascalientes and Baja California.

Blanca Hernández lost all hope of finding her son alive the day she spoke with someone connected to drug trafficking. “He told me, ‘Please, ma’am, don’t look for him anymore. You’re in grave danger. They’re going to kill you all.’”

Officially, Julio is one of the approximately 135,000 missing persons in Mexico, a crisis that has reached record numbers in recent years (with organized crime playing a central role). Only a year ago, this family laments, the Jalisco State Attorney General’s Office issued its first missing person report for Julio. “My brother became just another missing person, but for us, he will always be our family member,” Jessica says.

“It’s all been very hard”

The family fled to Tijuana, but even there, they didn’t feel safe. In 2024, they decided to cross into the United States to surrender to the Border Patrol. They all passed the first hurdle in their asylum application: the credible fear interview. Afterward, they remained in immigration custody — some for days, others for months — until they were released and able to reach their destination.

The process continued. They began to get settled in the United States, like so many other migrants. They attended hearings, confident that they had enough evidence to win their case. They even had copies of the complaints they had filed in Mexico. But on April 13, 2026, the family received a devastating blow: an immigration judge granted the government’s request to close their asylum application and denied them protections against deportation. She ordered that they be sent to Ecuador or, failing that, to Honduras. Guatemala was left as a third option.

These three nations have cooperation agreements with the Trump administration, functioning as “safe third countries,” meaning they receive migrants and process their asylum claims there. Human rights and immigrant advocacy groups, however, have questioned whether they genuinely meet the protection standards required under U.S. law. The agreements were initially signed during Trump’s first term, but were suspended during Joe Biden’s presidency. Trump reactivated them after returning to the White House. In the case of Ecuador, the agreement came back into force in July, 2025.

“It’s all been very hard,” Blanca Hernández laments. “I told the judge that we were in grave danger in Mexico, but that, between going to Ecuador or returning to Mexico, I’d rather die in Mexico.” She adds: “It’s not right that, just because of a mistake my eldest son made, more people are going to die. I am asking the U.S. government to give us a chance. We’re not bad people. We didn’t come here to steal. We didn’t come here to take anything from you.”

Her daughter, Alondra De Ávila, agrees that, if they’re deported to their home country, “we would have to live in hiding; there’s nowhere safe for us there.”

Their appeal against the immigration judge’s ruling has given them a glimmer of hope. The family is determined to pursue the legal fight through every possible level of appeal. “My family isn’t asking for money. We just want to be allowed to stay in this country,” Jessica insists. “It’s unjust to deny us that protection.”
